the rapporteur. - mr president, first of all, i would like to congratulate you on your election as president of this house. i wish you and the whole house the best for the next two and a half years. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the house is now voting on the directive on public procurement, supplies and services and on the directive on special sectors, namely water, energy and transport services. they come after four years of commission work, during which various hearings, studies and evaluations were carried out. they come after two more years of work in parliament, a very well attended public hearing and after hearing the committee of the regions, trade associations and professionals from all over europe. this is not surprising, given that public procurement in the union accounts for some 15% of total gdp, or more than eur 1 500 billion, each year. under the current directives, it is estimated that only 20% of this amount falls within the standards indicated by the directives, as the threshold value, above which their application is binding, is relatively high and in any case more or less equal to the agreements for the participation of third countries. the existing directives, which are outdated, need to be revised and adapted to new technologies and new market situations. the need to complete the internal market more and more prompted the commission to study and propose the directives in question. the matter is of considerable importance and could not and cannot be treated lightly. in addition to individual colleagues, four parliamentary committees for opinions and the committee responsible for legal affairs examined the texts and proposed amendments; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the contents can be summarised as follows: the commission has also proposed that the existing directives be revised and updated; that electronic purchasing mechanisms be introduced; that rules on technical specifications be clarified; that rules on award criteria be clarified; that thresholds be simplified; and that a common vocabulary for public procurement be introduced. the proposals are to be shared and are shared: we all know how important they are and we all want them to have a smooth ride. however, it is necessary to highlight the most important problems that have emerged and are the subject of debate within the individual political forces, between the political forces and between the national representations. the thresholds, i.e. the value below which compliance with the directives is not binding. this value is already relatively high, as i have pointed out, but it corresponds, as the commission proposes, to the value of the agreements with third countries. it has been proposed to raise that value. this poses a twofold problem: the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a directive on the protection of the environment in the event of a fire. it also states that the bodies responsible for calling for tenders will be able to operate outside the common rules with the associated risks. some point out that, despite the increase in thresholds, there will be no decrease in contracts awarded on a european basis because, below a certain value, firms find it not economically viable to move outside their own region, let alone outside their own country. a further consideration is whether each member state and each regional government can apply local rules below the thresholds. the higher the thresholds, the more differentiated the rules within the union will be and therefore the less uniform the rules within it will be. i believe that whatever the value of the thresholds, we must not allow the existence of different laws in the union. this would mean a reduction, not an expansion, of the common market; the commission has also proposed that the member states should be able to restrict access to the market for the services of non-local operators. this should only be done in so far as it is not provided for in the directives. it follows that the general content of the directives must also be understood in national or regional legislation, and an amendment has been proposed to that effect. another important issue is related to environmental and social aspects. some have proposed that the directive should supplement and contain specific rules in these areas. this has been the subject of extensive and thorough discussion and could be referred back to committee if a position is not reached at the vote with an adequate majority. i believe that legislation which is intended to implement the internal market in an economic field and to strengthen competitiveness cannot be based on principles which are not provided for in sectoral legislation. the commission proposal already contains appropriate references to ensure that all the principles relating to the environment and workers' rights are respected when drawing up the call for tenders. this legislation cannot be extended or amended by means of directives which must cover procurement, supplies and services. the amendments to this report, which were approved by a number of committees for opinions and the committee on the substance, are intended to introduce new rules. if these amendments were to be adopted in plenary, i believe it would be better to retain the existing texts rather than texts which, although more modern, risk bringing fundamental aspects back. there is another issue which these regulations cannot ignore and which the commission has not adequately addressed: the intellectual performance. it is time that a clear and sharp line was drawn between intellectual achievement and execution, between planning and execution. it is a concept which is difficult for certain trade associations to grasp, since they defend positions which have been established over time. but the intellectual work cannot be considered as the execution of a product nor can a company do everything, both design and execution, except in exceptional cases or for the use of specific technologies. and this for two reasons: the product of the invention is not quantifiable; one idea is never the same as another. the history of europe, century after century, is full of works of various kinds which have outlived their artistic value. not everything, not every performance can be compared to a work of art, but the product of the brain cannot be confused with mere execution. the executing firm has the skills and experience, the executive technology and, as such, is best placed to design and implement the technical ideas of others, but that is all, with a few rare exceptions. separating the intellectual services from the executive services does justice to the professions and the product of the intellect. integrated procurement, seen as the sum of executive design and execution alone, is appropriate if there are intellectual service providers within the enterprise, or connected to it, who are entitled to do so under the regulations in force. these considerations are the basis both for the amendment which does not impose the obligation of the union or separation between design and execution but requires justification for the union if it is used, and for the amendment which clearly defines what is meant by preliminary, final and executive design. finally, mr president, two directives are being tabled in parliament which are essentially similar in that certain specific sectors have been liberalized or will be liberalized in the not too distant future. telecommunications are already considered to be liberalised and are therefore not examined. the progressive liberalization of water, energy and transport matters, which the commission will be monitoring directly or at the request of individual member states, will make the second directive obsolete without having to amend the first. on the whole, i hope that non-partisan considerations will lead us to adopt rules which are specific to the sector without dangerous expansion; increasingly implement the internal market; taking into account that other countries are about to join the union with their own traditions and needs; the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. i also feel it is my duty to acknowledge that the work done by the commission with its proposal is worthy of the highest appreciation. finally, i am proud to have contributed to deepening and hopefully improving legislation which not only contributes to the creation of a more united and stronger europe but also represents a breakthrough in the fight against fraud and malpractice, which are very often the cause of economic problems. it is better to have a stop-gap directive than to have rules which leave too much discretion, if necessary, to avoid a wide net.

- mr president, this report traces the difficult paths which should link the necessary increase in the production of consumer goods and services with the requirements of environmental protection. i have appreciated the commission's proposal, the rapporteur's specificity, the severity and serenity with which she has dealt with the subject. every product has a life cycle that begins the moment it is made available to the consumer, who, by using it, immediately puts it in relation to its environmental sustainability, a somewhat difficult term but one that everyone understands today. it is a delicate relationship, which is not exhausted by the use and by the conclusion, so to speak, of the life of the good. the most serious problems often arise when the product, once it has ceased to function, has to be disposed of, retired, in other words, eliminated from the world in which it has served. this is where the most delicate environmental repercussions arise, because not all products are disposable with the same technology, nor do they all have the same degree of hazard or the same level of biodegradability. the commission therefore proposes an initiative which takes, as we say, the cake at the top: for an asset to be easily disposable at the end of its life cycle, it must be designed for this purpose from the very beginning, and this is the most valuable aspect of this report. the commission has therefore proposed that incentives be created to encourage preliminary studies on better information for producers on the technologies and the choice of raw materials suitable for this purpose. the proposal does not ignore an aspect which could become an obstacle to approaching the world of production: the costs. in fairly concrete terms, the text says that in addition to encouraging aid to producers who face higher costs in supplying these biodegradable goods, there must also be a pricing policy which allows them to differentiate the tariffs on the market and, once again, why not, to differentiate the tax burden as well. i mean, a watchful eye for those who are committed to helping the environment, to helping us.

- report (a5-0457/2001) by mr lavarra, on behalf of the committee on fisheries, on the communication from the commission to the council and the european parliament on the elements of a strategy for integrating environmental protection requirements into the common fisheries policy (com (2001) 143 - c5-0343/2001 - 2001/2143 (cos)).
the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i believe that the definition of a strategy to improve the integration of environmental protection requirements into the common fisheries policy is a priority requirement and therefore the commission deserves our appreciation for having prepared this communication. i believe, however, that we must see this communication as the starting point for a debate open to operators, researchers, political institutions and consumers. the integration of environmental needs into the common policy must be done in a way that is shared by the sector, without the costs being borne solely and exclusively by the sector itself, especially when it comes to small fisheries, especially when the sector is the victim of forms of pollution of the marine environment caused by external factors: the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve the situation of the coastal industry. i also believe that the integration of environmental requirements must be based on scientific principles and we hope to have precise data from the commission soon on the basis of the research that is being carried out. in the meantime we must certainly use the precautionary principle, but here too we must adopt measures which do not affect the income of small fisheries undertakings and which are also alternative to those proposed by the commission. in fact, when the commission refers to the interaction between fisheries and the environment, it sometimes merely emphasises the negative ecological effects of fisheries, while neglecting positive environmental measures that could benefit the fisheries sector: improvement of coastal areas, creation of re-population and nursery areas, marine protected areas, enhancement of fisheries-tourism and, more generally, investment in research. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. in the proposal contained in the report adopted by parliament's committee on fisheries, we therefore call on the executive to improve the coordination of research in the field of fisheries and marine ecology, not to reduce structural aid, to take greater account of the specific nature of the mediterranean, whose diversified, multispecies fisheries require appropriate regulatory measures. let me give you an example. we are not asking for derogations from the current prohibitions on the mediterranean, such as those on swordfish. we are asking, however, that agreements with third countries should prohibit or limit the use of this type of fishing, otherwise we would only create penalties for our fishermen, without at the same time solving the problem of over-exploitation of these resources. finally, i feel i should urge greater attention to eco-labelling, also in response to the alarm about dioxin in fishery products, which has affected consumer sensibilities.

the rapporteur. - mr president, with today's debate and tomorrow's vote in the house we have come to the end of a long and difficult journey which has involved the three institutions for some years in a frank and close debate on a subject of primary importance: the question of the future of the community. the information, consultation and participation of workers. the conciliation, which was successfully concluded on 17 december, established minimum standards for information and consultation to be applied throughout the union. this directive therefore complements - after those on european works councils, the european company statute and the charter of fundamental rights - the existing community and national framework, which can help to prepare for change, to ensure that restructuring takes place in an acceptable context, to give the employment objective the preeminence required in the current context. and it seems to me particularly significant that an agreement was reached before the barcelona summit. almost all member states have a legal framework, whether by regulation or by contract, to ensure that workers are informed and consulted: i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware of the fact that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. to cut to the chase: this directive recognises the right of workers and their representatives in all undertakings with fewer than 50 employees to be informed and consulted on all aspects of the life of the undertaking, with particular reference to the effects of the undertaking's choices on employment, work organisation, training and retraining. it is important that the directive focuses on the content and the arrangements, including the time-frame, for information and consultation. it is explicitly stated that these must be done in good time, as it is a prerequisite for the success of the restructuring and adaptation processes of enterprises and the identification of the necessary pre-return measures to avoid negative effects on workers. a number of rights are granted to workers' representatives and to the workers themselves; the court of first instance held that the principle of proportionality requires that the member states should, when implementing and applying the directive, introduce in their legislation penalties which are effective, proportionate and dissuasive. i think that is a particularly significant point, and there has been a lot of debate on this. the commission's initial forecast, supported by parliament, was for a european sanction. the directive provides instead for the member states to introduce the penalty themselves - thus respecting the principle of subsidiarity. there is also a transitional period for those states which have no legislation - neither legal nor contractual - a transitional period which, however, has been shortened compared with the common position. of course, the european parliament would have wanted more: i would have liked more precise information, a more precise definition, more content, but if we consider the sensitivity of the subject, the resistance which has been shown in recent months not only by governments but also by lobbies, i think we can be satisfied. parliament's delegation to the conciliation committee voted unanimously in favour of this hypothesis of agreement. we can be satisfied that rights are recognised, social dialogue is promoted, the principle of subsidiarity is respected, but that a uniform framework is defined throughout the union: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the social partners are able to take part in the negotiations. i would like to conclude by expressing my special thanks to the commissioner, mrs diamantopoulou, and her staff, and to the belgian presidency and to minister onkelinx. i would like to emphasize that there were three women, three of us in particular, involved in this directive. i believe that it was also our determination and our conviction of the great importance of the subject - supported by myself, my committee and parliament, and by the convictions of the commissioner and the minister - that enabled us to bring such a fundamental process to a conclusion. the barcelona summit will, in my view, be a good opportunity to see whether what we have concluded can have a concrete and positive effect.

- mr president, commissioner, in the united states - the country where the most striking results have been achieved in reducing cigarette consumption - the impact of taxation, as a percentage of the price, is far less than that of all european countries, even those with the lowest excise duties. i think that is a point of reference that we must bear in mind. there is another fact to be borne in mind. the british colleague said that the increase in prices leads to a decrease in cigarette consumption, and this is true. what has happened in italy, however, is that the increase in the price of cigarettes, induced by the increase in taxation, has officially reduced cigarette consumption, but simply because it has increased the consumption of contraband cigarettes to a very large extent. this is especially true because smuggling of cigarettes is not smuggling between european countries with different levels of excise duty - remember that in the united states excise duties on tobacco vary from state to state - but smuggling between outside europe and inside europe: it is the smuggling from montenegro across the adriatic and on this route across europe. and this problem of criminal, mafia smuggling is a problem which we risk exacerbating if we continue with this policy of increasing excise duties. the positive results in terms of public health achieved in the united states - i say this to my colleagues - have been pursued and achieved by applying excise duties which are in percentage terms lower than those in europe.

in writing. - (it) before i vote in favour of the report, i would like to stress the important contribution which mr von wogau has made to parliament's work as a member of the committee on economic and monetary affairs and the contribution he will continue to make to the committee on constitutional affairs. i congratulate you ! the process of integration of international financial markets involves the remodelling of all the structures which underpin financial services. in this context, the study of experience gained also on non-european markets in terms of the organization, operation and articulation of control measures is therefore gaining more and more weight. specific implementation therefore requires the use of new telematic technologies used to increase the efficiency of mobile markets. by increasing the level of competition between mobile operators and by managing a volume of trading in terms and times that were unprecedented until a few years ago, the use of these new instruments has increased the 'quality' of prices on these markets and reduced intermediation costs. the efficiency and integration of securities markets must, however, be achieved through a more efficient decision-making process - lamfalussy's example - by safeguarding the institutional balance in compliance with all established and operational levels of democratic control. that being so, the first point to be implemented is to facilitate and speed up the legislative process by approving legislative acts at first reading, as far as possible. secondly, we must strengthen transparency and information, which is a key platform for the creation of a new integrated european securities market. the third point is linearity and regularity, which should guide consumers and investors. it is therefore necessary to have an information system which assists the transactions, from the phase of issuing the order to the liquidation. finally, it is essential to have regulation of securities brokerage functions, which should be articulated in a discipline of intermediary subjects and a discipline of activities, in addition to a new structure in terms of supervisory powers, a structure within which parliament would have the same powers as the commission.

the rapporteur. - mr president, the convention which is about to open will not fulfil its mandate unless it gives convincing answers on a crucial point: the european parliament has a duty to ensure that the process of european integration is democratic. that is the starting point of the report, which was approved by the committee on constitutional affairs and is before parliament today in plenary. we all know how the convention must redefine the union's missions, its role in the world, in global development and peace-building, its policies of growth, cohesion, security in freedom and justice. but it is hard to consider everything else as purely institutional technicalities, abstract exercises of institutional engineering which cannot be of interest to the citizens. if the european cause has lost its support among the citizens, it is also because they have felt alien to too many decisions of the union, and have found it difficult to influence or even understand them. to regain consensus, it is essential to make clear to all decision-makers within the union how decisions can be made transparent, legible and verifiable, and by which institutions citizens can be effectively represented in europe. these are all questions of democracy, vital questions of democracy. the role of the parliamentary institution is fundamental to this end, although not in itself decisive. a clear and consistent choice is now required to strengthen the parliamentary institution in the union's architecture, to further parliamentarize the union, in addition to the progress already made in the 1990s. parliamentarisation must be based on two pillars, the european parliament and the national parliaments. both contribute equally to the democratic legitimacy of the european union as a union of citizens, of peoples and not just of states. i want to be clear: if we as a european parliament have been guilty of a certain exclusivism, we must rid ourselves of it. the european parliament must be free from any mutual distrust between the european parliament and the national parliaments. we must understand their concerns and suggest the right answers. the report i am presenting to you points in three directions: first, greater powers of direction and control for national parliaments vis-à-vis their respective governments and the effective exercise of those powers; secondly, closer and more systematic cooperation between the european parliament and the national parliaments, including through an interparliamentary agreement signed by the respective presidents. it is a new idea, and i am particularly pleased that the president of this parliament has taken the initiative. thirdly, the conferral of a constituent power on the national and european parliaments, shared with the governments and the commission, as in the convention - which is about to begin its work - on the revision of the treaties and, today, with the aim of a genuine european constitution. these are the valid solutions to be pursued, not those which would lead to confusing the roles of the european parliament and national parliaments and to further burdening the institutional architecture and decision-making mechanisms of the union. in particular - as a careful report by the house of lords has shown - a second chamber, composed of national parliamentarians, would be an unreal solution to some real problems. i hope very much that the spirit of this report will be understood and appreciated and that, with your agreement, the convention will benefit from our contribution.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i also share the views of my delegation and i think it was a wise choice to entrust the preparation of this report to mr giorgio napolitano, who was able to grasp well the concern about the imbalance between the powers attributed to the executive institutions and the possibilities granted to parliaments as a whole, one of the main aspects on which his report is based. the european parliament has been expressing this concern for years, mr president, and mr napolitano's report offers a first effective remedy, in full accordance with the maastricht treaty and the treaty of amsterdam. the second important aspect of the report concerns what i had the opportunity to point out months ago to the italian ambassador, even before anyone else, because it is a problem that is mainly italian, that of the incompatibility between the mandate of a european parliamentarian on the one hand, and that of a national parliamentarian, regional councillor and - i would humbly add, asking mr napolitano to take note of this - mayor of a large city on the other. if the european parliament is to regain its political role, the level of debate must be raised, as must the level of the presence of members of the european parliament in brussels and strasbourg. the third point i would like to stress is the intelligent and categorical rejection of a house composed of representatives of national parliaments in the report, in order to avoid a decision-making burden, but above all to better separate the different powers of the parliaments. we are therefore moving towards an institutional agreement which we hope president cox, accepting the invitation of mr napolitano, will be willing to initiate. we are moving towards a process of elevating the institutional role of parliaments, to which the art of politics and government is demanded by popular choice, against any decidedly antiquated aspect of the concentration of executive power in the hands of institutions that have no legitimacy whatsoever from the popular vote. i would like to take this opportunity to thank mr napolitano for his excellent and brilliant work.

the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, it must be stressed that this report is coming to parliament at a historical and political moment of particular importance for the construction of europe, namely on the eve of the start of the convention which will lay the foundations of the new europe, a convention of which commissioner barnier is an authoritative member. so we are particularly pleased to have him here with us tonight. i think it is important to stress once again that cohesion policy is one of the greatest achievements of the community integration process, one of the cornerstones of the community integration of yesterday, today and, i would say, tomorrow. as the commission has already done in its second report, we too have seen that in the objective 1 regions between 1988 and 1998 gdp per head rose from 63 to 70 per cent of the community average - and this is a great achievement - but cohesion has not only benefited the countries that used the funds, but also the net taxpayers, in the form of exports of goods and services. of course, the journey is not over. there is still much to be done, difficulties to be faced and overcome, especially unemployment, a scourge which unfortunately afflicts many regions, where its rate has not diminished at all. infrastructure investment is needed to overcome the territorial challenges and the peripherality of islands and outermost regions; the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve accessibility, which is a decisive factor in competitiveness, without incurring excessive costs in the environmental sector. the cohesion policy will have to be reshaped, firstly in the light of the new context that enlargement offers us all, and this in particular in the light of the conclusions reached by the commission in its documents, in particular in the last document, a few days ago, the so-called interim document. the gap between rich and poor will unfortunately widen, as after enlargement one sixth of the community's population will have an income of just 40 per cent of the community average. the applicant countries have been helped, they have been brought closer to the new reality, in which they will have to integrate, through accession instruments such as ispa and the sapard programme, which have represented an essential means for the transition from candidate countries to member states. but a genuine policy of territorial development must be promoted, and i believe that in this context the european space development scheme can be an important technical source of great integration and great development. the two fundamental requirements must be balanced, namely solidarity with the new countries, without penalising but rather protecting the current beneficiaries of cohesion policies. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for approval. statistical convergence cannot be confused with the real convergence of the present beneficiaries, who will not automatically become richer simply because poorer regions join. management arrangements are needed to improve the operation of the actions; a greater division of roles between the commission and the national and regional levels will have to be eliminated, promoted and encouraged; the need for further simplification of procedures will be felt; the commission has already made a number of proposals. it will also be essential to rationalise the instruments of intervention by reducing and decreasing funds and improving coordination between community and cohesion policies. objective 1 should be maintained for regions which will continue to lag behind in terms of development, measured not only by income per head but also by other criteria such as unemployment. finally, the financial allocation should be increased or at least revised, and this is a thorny subject on which there has been a great deal of debate. the 0.45% threshold cannot be lowered in any case. we hope that parliament, in conjunction with the commission, will be able to ask for an increase in the budget devoted to future cohesion policy resources.
- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, title xvii of the treaty establishing the european community, and in particular article 158, establishes among the political priorities of the union the 'harmonious development of the community as a whole', with the aim of 'reducing the disparity between the levels of development of the various regions and the backwardness of the less favoured or island regions'. i personally believe that we must continue to pursue this objective with a consistent, constant and sustainable policy. the second report on eu cohesion, presented by commissioner barnier, paints a picture of a situation which has improved but which is certainly not resolved. it is clear that progress has been uneven and that there are still strong regional disparities which - as the rapporteur rightly points out - are not diminishing but deepening. i fully support the position of my colleague, mr musotto, on the objectives. the criteria for selecting regions eligible for aid currently refer to the threshold of 75% of the community average of gdp per capita. i personally think that it would be more appropriate to identify the unemployment rate from 2006 onwards, since the entry of poorer regions and those most in need of aid will certainly not raise the level of the regions currently covered by objective 1.

- madam president, this resolution is intended to underline an essential point, namely that the fight against terrorism, which will be long and hard, must be conducted as far as possible in accordance with international law and the rule of law. this is a request from within american society and from this parliament itself, which i hope will approve this resolution. as regards the guantanamo detainees, who are part of the al qaeda network and who were captured in afghanistan, two problems arise. the first is the question of detention, since there is worrying evidence from the international red cross on the conditions of detention. the second concerns the legal status of prisoners: there is uncertainty about this, but it is clear that john walker, an american citizen, is being tried by a civilian court, while the other detainees are being tried by a secret military court. this is not acceptable. it 's probably true what general morillon says: the geneva conventions will also have to be updated, in the sense that the convention provides for the status of prisoners of war, but when that status is uncertain, it must also provide for the existence of prisoners of undeclared war, who should not therefore have less guarantees, less attention from the point of view of respect for human rights in the conditions of detention. the resolution also makes an important request that the un security council establish a competent tribunal for afghanistan, so that both the legal status of prisoners and the conditions of detention can be addressed. in approving this request, we are making a very sensible move which will, among other things, help to combat terrorism.

mr president, i congratulate mrs doris pack on her report on the socrates programme, which has given me the impetus for a number of considerations. we can safely say that the main objective of developing european citizenship and in particular of improving the quality of education systems has been fully achieved. this is demonstrated by the considerable benefits obtained from cultural openness, the overcoming of prejudices and cultural stereotypes and, consequently, the learning of languages enjoyed by the beneficiaries of the socrates grants. nevertheless, the analysis shows some weaknesses, such as the integration of the socrates programme with the comenius, lingua and leonardo da vinci programmes, which will require considerable adjustments and greater coordination and strengthening. one aspect which i think should be given very serious consideration is the financial support offered to the winners of socrates grants: the appropriation is insufficient to support the students, due to a criterion of quantitative distribution of grants which has resulted in an excessive reduction in the amounts available. there is a great diversity of national situations in a context of an overall reduction in the amount of grants awarded to each student, while the contribution of family members tends to increase. as the report has already pointed out, this trend clearly determines the risk of growing inequalities among students. in this connection, sufficient resources must be made available to enable the applicant to provide for himself independently, i.e. without the necessary support of his family, taking into account that the scholarships must not be differentiated, either in relation to the applicant's country or to the country to which he travels for the project. this economic discrimination would result in access to the programme being restricted to a group of individuals who can rely on family support. another major drawback of grant award is the bureaucratic financing procedure, which is currently lagging behind and will have to be remedied.
the commission is aware of the fact that the commission has not yet adopted a proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos. we would not be where we are if parliament had not helped. thank you very much . i also thank you, mrs pack, and all the other speakers for the positive assessment you have made of the youth programmes. it is true agree with everyone who says that this wonderful programme which is working very well, apart from a few minor problems here and there, needs to be developed. i also agree with those who say there is a again". but they also all tell me that the purse is too small. we know this and we would like the finance ministers, first of all, to give us more means, give us more opportunities so that we can mr president, mr mayol i raynal's report concerns the index of labour costs, which is of the utmost importance to be uniform throughout europe. this important regulation states that the labour cost index is divided into four points. article 4 of the regulation provides that the total of social contributions paid by employers and the taxes paid by them are to be shown under a single heading. no, mr president, i will not. the pensioners' party is opposed to this index of labour costs. taxes are one thing, pension contributions are another. we need to know how much the worker's pension affects the cost of labour and how much the taxation affects it. if we don't distinguish, we'll never solve the pension problem.
in writing. - (it) we must of course appreciate the content of the mayol i rainal report, on which we voted in favour, just as we appreciate the commission's intention - following the request of the ecofin council in september 2000 - to finally give life to a labour cost index whose validity and applicability, supported by a legal basis, are recognised throughout the union. the question is, however, how the commission will approach future data and how it will be objectively considered. the commission's text is particularly puzzling in that it states that labour costs can be a factor in inflation. the rapporteur raises a further question because, in the final analysis, the question to be asked in this context is whether four areas alone can be sufficient to provide all the answers to the complexity of the information that is sought. for example, the weight within a productive category of the cost of labour per unit of output - linked as it is to the rate of utilisation of the facilities - will be common to all, as will the importance of its geographical location. another point: it would be necessary to establish whether regions which may be penalized by high unit labour costs benefit from state aid or from the structural funds and to make provision for monitoring these cases to check whether their effect is dynamic and positive over time or, on the contrary, is immobilizing. this involves determining the effect of cohesion policies in one case or of the free choice of entrepreneurs in the face of opportunities in the other. finally, apart from the trend in imported tariffs and inflation rates, account should be taken of the fiscal and parafiscal characteristics of each country, because, while agreeing with the rapporteur, we believe that there is no member state whose contractual dynamics a priori determine a cost of living index which stimulates the cost of living. the truth is that in recent years contractual dynamics have ceased to be a means of distributing wealth and that they are sometimes unable to compensate fully for the effects of inflation in retrospect. in conclusion, these are the checks that should be carried out if, as the commission wishes, the social partners are to be given more appropriate instruments for wage negotiations. it is, however, comforting to think that these already have the comparisons cited for their objective assessments.

the commission is aware of the seriousness of the situation in the gulf and is therefore prepared to take action. i think this is a good opportunity to also mention the initiatives which the commission has taken on these issues in recent weeks. as you know, the international conference on financing for development in monterrey will be held immediately, the world summit on sustainable development in johannesburg will be held in september and we must define our position on both issues. much has been written about the perceived antagonism between the porto alegre world social forum and the new york world economic forum. in both cases, actors from different cultural and ideological backgrounds, from different environments, have come together. the world economic forum has certainly provided a good platform for a broad, well-founded and unbiased debate on issues of urgent concern to the whole world. some commentators claim that the porto alegre meeting, however, was more important than the new york meeting. it was argued that the real world civil society was in brazil and not in new york. i would not deny the attendees of the world economic forum for development the right to be considered as part of civil society. but it is true that the social forum was a significant meeting, an important event which policy makers will have to take into account in a clear way from now on. i would conclude, however, that not all the participants who gathered in porto alegre took a stand against globalisation. i think, rather, that they are even part of this phenomenon of globalization, which has allowed, thanks to new technologies, non-governmental movements, to have a global impact. it is another thing to criticize a capitalist model which can lead to undermining social cohesion and to an exhaustion of natural resources. in this respect, the views and concerns of davos and porto alegre may not be so different. achieving a balance between the global economic and social process and the preservation of our planet's resources is a great responsibility and a difficult task that no one person or country can manage alone. the solutions are difficult and complex. easy solutions are sometimes popular, but they tend to silence the side effects and the painful choices and trade-offs that politics often involves. the complexity of the real solutions often leads to a lack of understanding on the part of social movements and even of political leaders. we therefore consider it essential that in-depth studies be carried out, which make it possible to clarify, explain things well and communicate them clearly. the commission has attempted to make such an effort through its report 'answers to the challenges of globalisation'. we put aside any kind of prejudice and the study takes a series of proposals for reform of the international financial architecture as they are raised in the academic and political debate in the world today, and puts it in the perspective in which we find ourselves. while acknowledging that globalisation has many other facets, including the social and environmental dimension, the report focuses primarily on the international financial and monetary system and the problems of financing development. the report began by analysing the evolution of the globalisation process in the economic sphere and identifying some of the challenges related to the financial and monetary system. the report recognises the benefits of international economic integration, but also notes the existence of systemic deficiencies and that poverty reduction remains a major problem. it confirms the need for more and more effective official development assistance. the report recognises that many countries have achieved an increase in their per capita income and an improvement in their quality of life that would not have been achieved with a less integrated strategy. it also reflects the strong increase in foreign direct investment, a key factor in boosting growth and, consequently, in combating poverty. the report examines several existing proposals on international taxation. as regards the general use of these taxes as a potential source of development finance or public goods, we conclude that, while some of them will appear attractive for short and medium-term needs, there are not many alternatives to funding from national budgetary resources. this conclusion implies a re-alignment of priorities within the budgetary allocations. another proposal of interest is the introduction of a tax on monetary transactions. the report considers two perspectives: firstly, with regard to the so-called 'tobin tax' as a tool for stabilising the foreign exchange markets, the analysis leads us to the conclusion that it is difficult to assume that such a tax will contribute substantially to the stability of exchange rates. however, if we look at this instrument as a tool to increase the resources available for financing development, the tobin tax may be more attractive. it is true that its implementation would be laborious, since it would require almost global coverage to minimise tax evasion and would require a strong international consensus. even if such a consensus could be reached at political level, numerous technical problems would still arise, such as those relating to the appropriate tax base and collection mechanisms. these results are substantially in line with the resolution on the international monetary system adopted by the european parliament last autumn. another important aspect of the report is the finding that for many developing countries trade technical assistance and capacity building are important in seizing growth opportunities from trade. ladies and gentlemen, the european union is well placed to play a leading role in promoting sustainable global development. it is the world's largest donor of development aid, the world's largest trading partner and a major source of foreign direct investment. in addition, as part of its commitment to protecting the environment, it is developing and promoting the use and dissemination of environmentally friendly technologies both within and outside europe. the european integration model has been developed along the lines of mutually supportive strategies for stable economic growth, social development and environmental protection. building on these achievements and in view of the forthcoming world summit on sustainable development in johannesburg, the commission has drawn up the communication towards a partnership for sustainable development. it is intended to identify the strategic components that form the basis of a global deal for johannesburg, with a view to getting all partners, both north and south, to work together towards sustainable development. the communication underlines several key priorities and makes concrete proposals for action in the economic, social and environmental fields. the commission and the member states have committed themselves to negotiate in a constructive spirit within the wto framework in order to continue the process of establishing a fair and free market trading system, in accordance with the conclusions of the doha ministerial conference. our aim is to raise the global standard of living through trade liberalization and development. the community actively promotes the participation of developing countries, and in particular the least developed countries, in the international trading system. the 'everything but arms' initiative is an important step in this direction, but it is not enough and we invite others to follow our example and improve market access for the least developed countries. we also take measures to support developing countries' efforts to integrate into and benefit from the global trading system. in line with the doha development agenda we have also recommended to member states to increase trade-related aid. the european union is also contributing to the international effort to strengthen the resilience of the international financial and monetary system and to reduce the potential for abuse for terrorist financing, money laundering and other illicit financial activities. the union will continue to focus its development policy on the overriding objective of poverty reduction. it will allocate its resources accordingly and ensure that european aid is used effectively. real practical progress in the quality and effectiveness of aid could be achieved if the rules governing policies and procedures were better harmonised, both at community level and in the member states. however, while not forgetting the need to increase efficiency, the commission believes that there is a gap between the resources needed to achieve the millennium development goals and the agreed timelines and means currently available. in the interests of the success of the monterrey conference on financing for development, the commission has therefore recommended to the council that the volume of official development assistance be increased and we suggest that by 2006 all countries whose aid to national income is below the eu average of 0.33% should be at this level. if we achieve this target, the union average would then rise to almost 0.4%, which would become a new threshold for the member states of the union, which, with this increase, could make a significant contribution to the achievement of the millennium development goals. moreover, a strong commitment to this gradual approach would strengthen the union's position in negotiating a fruitful international distribution of cargo. finally, as regards the overall protection of the environment, the commission proposes to launch an initiative on sustainable water management. we have committed ourselves to pressing our partners to achieve a 50% replenishment of the global environment facility by april 2002 and to extend its mandate. we are promoting the implementation of multilateral environmental agreements, including the ratification of the kyoto protocol, which member states have already done earlier this month. i think that, generally speaking, as industrialized countries, we have no right to demand that developing countries do more to protect the planet if we are not prepared to respect our own commitments. ladies and gentlemen, building a sustainable future for the world requires the collaboration of all. however, real progress can only be made if the main partners commit themselves to playing a crucial role and in this respect i am convinced that we, as the european union, must and can play that key role. let 's hear it .

the rapporteur. mr president, the decision we are dealing with is - i hope - the last necessary step towards the appointment of a european authority which will guarantee the protection of the privacy of european citizens, including in relation to the community institutions and bodies. the treaty of amsterdam, in article 286, provided that this should take place from 1999 onwards. we are late and must therefore avoid further delay. fortunately, after intensive joint work, regulation no 45/2001 of the european parliament and of the council was adopted at first reading, which established the principles and rules corresponding to those laid down for the member states by community directives for the processing of personal data by the community institutions and bodies. the regulation also established the independent supervisory authority, the european data protection supervisor, assisted by an additional data protection officer who ensures the application of the regulation. it laid down its tasks and functions - investigative, advisory, regulatory, conflict resolution - and the procedures for its appointment. the only two points which are not covered by the regulation are: the remuneration of the guarantor and his deputy and the seat of the body. as regards remuneration, since it is a body whose full independence is guaranteed, with supervisory functions over all the community institutions and bodies, it is very appropriate, in my view, to propose that the ombudsman should be paid the same as the ombudsman and the judges of the court of justice, while the assistant ombudsman, appointed by the same procedure and for the same period as the ombudsman, with the task also of replacing him in the event of his absence or incapacity, should be treated in the same way as the registrar of the court of justice. as regards the seat, since most of the departments responsible for the processing of personal data by the community institutions and bodies are located in brussels, it is rightly proposed that the seat of the data protection officer should be in brussels. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the budgetary resources available for the community are used to the full. other amendments, on the other hand, recall the adoption of another important regulation, regulation no 1049/2001, which concerns public access to european parliament, council and commission documents. these amendments, in so far as they introduce recitals and not new provisions, which would be inadmissible for lack of a legal basis, seem to me to be acceptable. the adoption of these two important regulations in the same year confirms that in europe the culture of the protection of individuals' personal data and the culture of transparency of public activities are growing together and not in opposition. both are opposed to the authoritarian and bureaucratic culture which, on the one hand, does not respect the privacy of individual citizens and, on the other, claims to keep the administrative procedures and activities of public bodies confidential. i believe that the adoption of this decision will be a decisive step in the system of protection of the fundamental right of european citizens to the confidentiality of their personal data, which is now enshrined in article 8 of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union.

the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. i would first of all like to thank the rapporteur, mr isler béguin, the committee on the environment, public health and consumer affairs, the committee on agriculture and rural development, the committee on fisheries and the committee on development and cooperation for their work on the draft report and this resolution. biodiversity is a key issue in sustainable development and the integration of environmental considerations into other policies. it is important in itself, but it also forms the very basis of natural resource-based activities such as agriculture and fisheries. biodiversity is also an important natural resource on which local communities in many countries depend for their livelihoods. at the same time, however, it is declining at a rate unprecedented in human history. i have some very sad news for you tonight. we have now lost the first species on our list of protected species. the pyrenean mountain goat has disappeared forever. we are thus not even able to fully protect the species we have placed on our lists of species we have promised to protect. both the eu's sustainable development strategy and the sixth environment action programme set as a central objective the halt of biodiversity loss by the year 2010. if we are to achieve this, it is very important that the action plans for biodiversity which we are discussing today are actually implemented. the full implementation of the birds and habitats directives is a prerequisite for the conservation of biodiversity. but that's not enough. if we really want to stop the loss of biodiversity, we need to look at the whole of the eu, not just the protected areas. it is necessary to integrate the issue of biodiversity into policies relating to the development and exploitation of land and sea. the biodiversity action plans are not only ambitious but also realistic. they represent a major step forward in integrating biodiversity into agricultural, fisheries and development cooperation policies and our own environmental policy. the action plan for the conservation of natural resources clearly demonstrates our firm intention to fully implement the birds and habitats directives and to support the work on natura 2000. it also sets out how we intend to use general environmental management tools such as environmental impact assessment, eco-labelling, environmental auditing and other economic management tools to promote the conservation of biodiversity across the eu. the agricultural action plan sets out priorities for achieving mutual benefits from agricultural activities and biodiversity. the main instruments range from rural development measures to the environmental aspects of the common organisation of the market, the beef, milk and cereals schemes, etc. the action plan covers all our rural areas, including natura 2000 sites. the fisheries action plan addresses threats from both traditional fisheries and aquaculture and is fully in line with the green paper on the future common fisheries policy. most of the most serious threats to global biodiversity are in developing countries. the fight against biodiversity is therefore closely linked to our strategy to eradicate poverty. we have a responsibility to assist developing countries in preserving the natural resources that are essential to their well-being. the economic cooperation and development action plan provides the tools for this. these biodiversity plans are not static instruments but will be developed mainly through the use of various indicators. this has been pointed out in the debate and is of course also something that the commission supports and that we have started to work on. these plans will contribute in particular to the debate on the reform of the common fisheries policy, the agricultural policy and the regulations on the structural funds. i hope that these reforms will have the scope and provide the necessary steering to enable us to fully achieve the objectives of the biodiversity action plans. only then can we achieve the overall objective of halting biodiversity loss by 2010. i thank all members for their valuable contributions to the debate.

commission. – mr president, i would like to express my satisfaction at the outset at the progress that has been made on this proposal for a directive on food supplements. first of all, the objective of this legislation – and i must emphasise this – is not to ban food supplements. it has to do with maximum safety levels. i regret very much that i have to disagree with my friend mr bowis, for whose opinions i have the utmost respect, when he says that the position at the moment is that there are upper safe limits. that really is not the position. this will be the position after this legislation comes into place. that is the purpose of the exercise. this exercise will be based on scientific evidence and scientific evaluation. it also dismays me to some extent to hear people in this house – also for whom i have enormous respect – express the view that this legislation is motivated by, of all things, lobbying of the pharmaceutical industry. that is a slander. it is absolutely wrong. it is unfair to say that i or the people who work for me would be motivated by such things. but sometimes people who make these allegations are the ones who are inordinately concerned about the role of industry. but what about the role of industry that profits from this piece of legislation not going through? the regulation of food supplements in the european union. it is designed to ensure that a very wide range of such products is available to consumers. the underlying criterion for a single market in food supplements is safety: adequate and appropriate labelling designed to inform consumers. of course, these products must be used in the context of a diversified diet and in line with manufacturers' instructions. the deadline for preparing dossiers for the evaluation of substances that are already on the market is an important issue. i have listened carefully to the concerns expressed, concerning to consider an extension of the period mentioned. i can, therefore, accept any one of amendments nos 1, 3, 4 or 5 that relate to this point, provided that this would contribute to the adoption of the common position without further changes. i have also taken careful note of the interventions with regard to good manufacturing practice for food supplements, which is the subject of amendment no 2. i would like to reiterate what i said at first reading. the adoption of principles of good manufacturing practice by legally binding measures for specific categories of products is not appropriate in the case of foodstuffs. this already exists in relation to foodstuffs in many pieces of horizontal legislation. i am happy to take comfort from mr nisticò's contribution on the basis that he is certainly one of the meps i know here who is a scientist himself. he supports this legislation. he has asked me to take careful note of the risks to ensure the elimination of low-quality products when this framework legislation goes through the system. i am happy to say that will be taken into account. the vast majority of these principles are covered by horizontal legislation, particularly in the directives on hygiene and control. these will apply also to the manufacture of food supplements. in the draft directive, we are referring specifically to the issue of purity criteria for the vitamins and minerals to be used. we have improved the relevant provisions following your amendment at first reading. we also foresee adopting specific technical rules with regard to the margins of tolerance for the amounts of vitamins and minerals declared to be present in food supplements. we believe that these rules are important for ensuring the quality of these products. i am firmly of the view that this array of horizontal and specific rules fully covers all concerns expressed that these products should be manufactured to high-quality standards. i cannot, therefore, accept amendment no 2 to adopt provisions on gmps for food supplements. however, i reiterate that i will give priority to adopting the technical rules on margins of tolerance mentioned in article 9(1). amendment no 6 refers functioning of the standing committee on the food chain and animal health and of the scientific panels of the european food safety authority. i believe that these issues are adequately covered in the recently adopted general food law. they should not, therefore, be repeated in this specific directive. for this reason i cannot accept amendment no 8. but i repeat and emphasise that the role of the would help the adoption of the directive at second reading. the commission cannot accept amendments nos 2, 6 and 8 and certainly does not support amendment no 7, that calls for the rejection of the common position.

from her personal commitment and determination. i am greatly encouraged that all three institutions are in general agreement on three key principles: the requirement that only animal by-products derived from animals fit for human consumption should be used in feed, cosmetic and pharmaceutical products; the prohibition of intra-species recycling; and the need to tighten certain provisions in order to improve the control and traceability of animal by-products. however, i regret that, despite the very good progress made on the proposal, the question of how to deal with catering waste remains a main obstacle to final agreement. the feeding of catering waste carries a major threat of transmission of serious animal diseases such as foot and mouth disease and classical swine fever. for example, the outbreak of foot and mouth disease in the uk last year, which caused such enormous losses to both the farming and non-farming community, is reliably known to have originated from swill feeding. i might also add that the outbreak of classical swine fever in the netherlands in 1997 was also caused by the feeding of pigswill in neighbouring germany. nobody would wish this to occur again. given the huge damage which has arisen from recent outbreaks of these diseases, the insistence of member states on very high levels of protection is understandable and shared by the commission. i am fully aware of your concerns that a total ban may not be appropriate, especially in member states with strict controls. however, i am equally aware that the member states are not prepared to take any risk arising from the authorisation of swill feeding. they have already decided on a ban in the swine fever directive, despite several opportunities to reconsider the need for a ban. there are no indications of a reversal of this position. parliament must also accept that there are contradictions in any proposal to retain swill feeding. for example, parliament is demanding the full traceability of ingredients in animal feedingstuffs and a ban on what might be described as cannibalism. how can this be consistent with a derogation allowing the use of waste collected from restaurants and hospital kitchens to feed pigs and poultry? similarly, how can parliament ask to exclude catering waste from the strict control rules of the regulation, fearing that these rules would compromise the practice of composting, and at the same time demand that the commission propose a new regulation on the safe disposal of catering waste? the commission, having heard the insistence of 13 member states on the necessity for a ban, and in the interests of consistency, remains opposed to any relaxation of an outright ban in this regulation. we must therefore reject amendments nos 1, 10 and 25. we are also opposed to these amendments on institutional grounds, as the insistence on a deadline and on the content of future proposals undermines the commission's right of initiative. furthermore, the disposal and recycling of catering waste is and will be governed by existing and future environmental legislation on biodegradable waste. finally, the commission has already officially declared that it is ready to propose transitional measures, to be adopted by comitology whenever this is justified and appropriate, in order to allow the affected industries time to adapt to the new requirements introduced by this regulation. i would also refer you to article 32, which might give further assistance in this area. turning to the details, we cannot accept amendments nos 3 and 5 on the requirement of the marking of unprocessed category 1 and 2 material. acceptance would require the marking of cadavers, including pet animals, and 1.2 billion tonnes of manure. i leave to your imagination the potential for the eurosceptic press to exploit this requirement in order to undermine our credibility. we also cannot accept amendment no 9, as detailed and sufficient requirements regarding accompanying documents and record-keeping are established in the annex to the regulation and may be supplemented if need be by comitology. we can, however, accept amendments nos 22 and 23 on catering waste making reference to environmental legislation, as they would ensure that the goals of the regulation are achieved without undermining separate collection schemes. therefore, amendments nos 17 and 19 are unnecessary and cannot be supported by us. amendments nos 22 and 23 also clarify that the highest risk catering waste from international means of transport should remain subject to the control rules of article 7. therefore, they are preferable to amendments nos 7 and 8. we cannot accept amendment no 18, aimed at excluding household kitchen waste from the definition of catering waste, as this is would be inconsistent with the existing eu legislation on classical swine fever. turning to another important issue – sludge from slaughterhouses – we cannot support the first part of amendment no 2, as it virtually destroys the effect of article 4 by removing from the scope of the article material from waste-water systems from all slaughterhouses and other premises from which specified risk material is removed. it should be noted that the tse regulation does not establish any rules in this area. but as an aside, and in answer to mr goodwill, i should point out that i have written to dr. jackson on this particular subject. i have sent a copy of the letter to a number of members and i will ensure that a copy is sent to you. it explains the position with regard to sludge and gives the kind of reassurance you sought earlier in your presentation. we could accept in broad terms the second part of amendment no 2, which seeks to clarify that animal material collected when treating waste water is a category 1 material only if contains bse specified risk material. however, amendment no 21, which has the same objective but is clearer, is acceptable. amendment no 4 cannot be accepted as, when combined with amendment no 2 or with amendment no 21, it would be superfluous and confusing. we cannot support amendment no 14, which would provide a 3-year transitional period without conditions to apply during this period. i repeat that the commission has already officially declared that it is ready to propose transitional measures to be adopted by comitology whenever this is justified and appropriate. we can support amendment no 24 aiming to extend the derogation on the feeding of certain animals with category 1 material to endangered and protected species of, for example, vultures. we cannot accept amendment no 11, as it would extend that derogation to any endangered or protected species. we can support amendment no 20 requiring member states to submit a report on the implementation of the regulation, except for the reference to the lifting of the ban on meat- and bonemeal. this is already comprehensively covered by the tse regulation. similarly, we can support the principle of amendment no 13, which has the same objective as the first part of amendment no 20, subject to editorial change. finally, we can accept amendments nos 6, 12, 15 and 16 to various articles and annexes, as they are in line with the basic objectives of the regulation. i wish also to note that parliament has not made any further amendments to the second proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council amending council directives 90/425/eec and 92/118/eec as regards health requirements for animal by-products.

the rapporteur. - mr president, mr president-in-office of the council, mr commissioner, there seems to be a slow recovery in economic growth, although the timing and the extent of this recovery are still uncertain, both in the united states and in europe. above all, this recovery is already highly diversified according to the various sectors concerned and is interwoven with restructuring and modernisation processes perhaps supported by strong public investment and by unacceptable protectionist measures, as is the case with steel in the united states. the problem facing the european union, however, is to prevent such a contradictory and differentiated recovery from coinciding, through the wait-and-see attitude of european and union governments, with the widening, rather than narrowing, of the innovation and competitiveness gap which already hurts europe compared to the united states. for this reason, the report i am presenting stresses the urgency of adopting - hopefully at the barcelona summit - a proactive policy and, above all, following the lisbon indications, a policy mix that makes the social agenda, as approved in nice, an integral part of a coordinated economic and social policy and focused on the objective of increasing the working population and full employment. this need is all the more acute when one considers the need to respect the constraints of the stability pact and, in particular, that of a budget deficit not exceeding 3 per cent of gross domestic product, which leaves very modest resources available for an anticyclical economic policy of the individual states. we therefore stress that it is not a question of concentrating new powers in brussels, but of making very selective choices and coordinating the intervention of the states in such a way as to achieve, at european level, a positive and synergistic critical mass of public intervention and private investment. so it is a matter of choice. in the report we support the need to give priority to the revival of an investment policy rather than to an undifferentiated reduction in the tax burden, except for further control of the cost of labour. in the field of public and private investment, we insist that the lisbon strategy be resumed, which is currently experiencing, especially in some countries, serious and worrying delays. this means giving priority to community resources and national investment in strategic areas such as research and innovation, lifelong learning as an integral and inseparable part of structural reform of the labour market, and the creation of a european network of infrastructures and services, starting with telecommunications. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we must not only hope for, but promote coordination, for example by proposing - as the executive commission - forms of open cooperation between different governments on joint projects on research, innovation, lifelong learning, active ageing policies, the latter being a condition for a reform of social security systems which is not disastrous for the pension treatment of workers. the social dialogue must also be involved in this policy mix, starting from the need to define the guidelines and forms of financing of continuing training policy. the involvement of the social partners in shaping a modern welfare state, making it a decisive factor in sustainable development towards full employment, is one of the essential features of the european social model. we must therefore reject all attempts in barcelona to weaken collective bargaining and to strip the charter of fundamental rights of a large part of its content.
