the rapporteur. - madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking my colleagues in the committee on economic and monetary affairs, who have contributed, particularly during the debate and then with a large number of amendments, to the improvement of this report and, i believe, to the definition of a text which i hope will satisfy both the committee and the house. the report gives an overall favourable opinion on the two commission communications: the first on tax policy strategies and the second on a strategy for a consolidated tax base for pan-european companies; the commission has adopted a favourable overall assessment of both the identification of the general objectives and the instruments which can be used to achieve them. the report's introduction points out that the steady growth in the tax burden over the last 20 years - which has only slightly decreased but has not ended in the last few years - is likely to be one of the reasons for the low growth in the european union. the commission, in its communications, in stressing that a certain level of tax competition could be unavoidable and contribute to a reduction in tax burdens, appropriately recognises the positive role of tax competition in the context of rules to prevent misconduct. the report restates and emphasizes the principle of fiscal competition, recalling that it is compatible, as the experience of recent years has shown, with a constant coordination of tax regulations aimed at eliminating obstacles to the completion of the internal market. tax competition is compatible with the completion of the internal market, which does not imply an absolute equalization of conditions of competition, and tax competition is only one of many variables which determine the competitive environment in each country and between countries. tax competition, as nobel prize winner mundell, one of the acknowledged fathers of the single currency, has said, is not contradictory even with the introduction of the euro. in addition, as regards tax competition, it must be stressed that in reality there is no race to the bottom, the race to the bottom in tax revenue that many people often fear, fearing the risk of running out of the resources needed by the states. we have seen that, in a system of tax competition, taxation has actually continued to grow in the last decades in the european union. we have been concerned - and the report is aware of this - about the tax burden on labour, but it is not proved, it is not rational to think that this is a consequence of a reduction in the tax burden on capital: this is not found in the data we have in front of us. i now move on to other points, mr president, mr commissioner. the report stresses the need to create a system which fully applies the principle of the country of origin - priority for the definitive system - on which the commission's documents are, in our view, still evasive. this objective is identified, but no timetable or method for introducing the country of origin system is given. the report welcomes some suggestions for improving the current system, but calls for the introduction of a definitive system. the report also refers to the commission's proposal for a directive on the harmonization of excise duties on alcohol and tobacco. as regards environmental protection, it is recognized that not only does the polluter pays principle apply, but that this principle is not limited to taxation. as regards energy taxation, i would point out that the current distortions of competition and asymmetries in the energy markets make it at least premature to propose tax harmonization for energy products. in the field of direct taxation, mr commissioner, the report hopes that the road to full implementation of the measures contained in the tax package can be completed as soon as possible and, in particular, that those rules which, by discriminating between residents and non-residents, leave room for fraud and are not compatible with the single market, will be removed. as regards the strategy for introducing a consolidated tax base for european-sized activities of companies, the report welcomes the commission's choice and proposes the adoption, at least temporarily, of the principle of home state taxation pending the consolidated base, stressing that the determination of rates, the level of taxation, should be left to the individual countries. finally, as regards instruments, i welcome the effort to introduce soft legislation and thus self-regulation by the member states. finally, i would like to stress the principle of parliament's codecision in tax matters and the transition to qualified majority voting for administrative matters, but not for the definition of rates and the tax base. i am in favour of both amendments as rapporteur.

individual member states. that resolution has since made explicit reference to the need to give the union legal personality. we cannot anticipate the convention, but this resolution gives a strong impetus to a constituent process which, in our view, is responsible for the future of democratic europe.
mr president, the carnero gonzález report raises a fundamental question at the right time, and the question of the legal personality of the union is an important aspect of that question. what is this question, it is soon said: the need to finally give the european union a face, a clear profile. you see, not so long ago, we were told, watch out for the road! the construction of europe has proceeded in disguise, without revealing its lines and its aims, relying on ambiguities calculated to reduce resistance and to avoid the most severe opposition. for decades, therefore, there has been a succession of partial achievements, de facto solidarities, to use an expression dear to jean monnet and engraved in the schuman declaration of 9 may 1950. it has gone on like this, without too many definitions of the political and institutional subject which was growing, without too many claims to coherence in the development of european construction. well, we say, "i'm not going to do it. the time has come for clarity, the time has come for the transition to an explicit characterization of the supranational entity which has gradually taken shape until it has a single currency. the convention will have to say what we are and what we want. the fact that the community has been an original construction, without historical precedent and without preconstituted models, cannot mean that it remains something ineffable, indefinable, much less that it remains monotonous. we must respond to legitimate citizens' questions and present ourselves as a union with its own design, with clear institutional balances, with a constitution, with a strong international role and therefore with a legal personality. hence the substantial and convincing reasoning behind the proposal by mr carlos carnero gonzález, which the committee on constitutional affairs fully endorsed.

in writing. - (it) taxation of savings has always been the subject of long debates. some advocate a withholding taxation, which is based on a taxation that is conclusive as to the tax situation of the person concerned. others support a more current position, which is that of communication; in this case, the taxable person does not terminate his tax liability because he will be subject to a subsequent levy in his annual return. from the point of view of fairness, this second method undoubtedly assures the community that income, whatever it may be, is taxed in full. but it is only fair if it is applied by everyone. the moment a member state, for historical reasons or expediency, considers that it should not do so, it destroys the basis on which this method is based. all this applies to the pérez royo report, which bases the taxation of crossborder savings on communication. for this directive to be implemented effectively, it must be applied when third countries subscribe to it. the agreement with third countries is therefore a prerequisite for the entry into force of the directive. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a decision on the conclusion of the agreement on the conclusion of the agreement on the free movement of goods and services between the european community and the republic of turkey.

in writing. - (it) tobacco cultivation plays a leading role, especially in the less favoured regions of europe. some 130 000 owners and 400 000 seasonal workers are involved in the production and processing of tobacco in the eu. these figures alone justify and call for a study of the social costs of the removal of aid before entering into the political debate on the future of this crop in the eu. on the other hand, restrictive action on tobacco crops in europe would have no effect on consumption, except to divert european smokers to non-community tobacco, which is much less well known and certainly more harmful to health. in addition, commission document com ((2001) 264 of 15 may 2001 on sustainable development stresses that 'decision-makers must identify and take into account any impact - positive or negative - in other areas. a thorough study of all the implications of a draft proposal should include an assessment of its economic, environmental and social effects within the eu and in third countries.' that is why, as european republicans, we believe that the commission should seriously promote studies and research on possible alternative crops that preserve the rural fabric in a sustainable way. we agree with the rapporteur that the political debate on tobacco should be postponed until parliament has to consider an evaluation report on the management of the fund, possibly containing a proposal for amendment and improvement. for all these reasons, we say no to the gradual elimination of subsidies to european tobacco growers, which was decided on blindly, we ask that the current levels of activities of the research fund be maintained for the period 2002-2004, because agronomic research is now one of the most important ways of making tobacco consumption less harmful to health, and we support the amended report by the committee on agriculture.

the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, we are all very familiar with the history of this framework decision. we have been consulted a second time because the framework decision on which we had already expressed our views two years ago has been revised. in the meantime, however, the commission has made a general reservation on the framework decision, noting that the subject of environmental protection is covered by numerous community texts, most of which provide for administrative sanctions, and therefore considers that the matter should be dealt with by a first pillar instrument. the commission insists that the existing sanctions have proved insufficient, as is shown by the state of the environment in europe. the proposal for a directive, which will be discussed in the context of mrs oomen-ruijten's report, must therefore be seen as complementary to the draft framework decision. the commission considers that a first pillar instrument should be adopted and that this instrument should take precedence over a third pillar instrument. this means that, when a matter falls within the community's competence, it is not legally possible for the union to adopt common rules through a third pillar instrument without infringing the powers of the community itself. i would remind you that parliament agrees with the commission on this point: at the sitting on 15 november 2001, we adopted a recommendation on criminal sanctions and community law, in a non-discussion procedure, calling on the council, in particular in paragraph 6, not to take any action on criminal law in environmental matters until the proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment by means of criminal sanctions has been adopted. now, these two documents - the framework decision and the directive - complement each other and are designed to be together, so as to avoid the schizophrenia of having two documents saying different things about the same subject. as you will see in the amendments, the framework decision refers specifically to the directive for the purposes of definitions and penalties, because we are convinced that the directive is the necessary and useful instrument, precisely because it is a community instrument, to protect the environment from devastation. i must also add a very important aspect: the council's framework decision would in fact impose criminal penalties when the environment has already been devastated, or at any rate irreparably damaged. we do not have the time here, of course, but we have already made this difference in philosophy very clear in committee. i therefore insist that we vote in favour of both the framework decision, which has already been adopted in committee, and the directive, because these two documents are complementary in this way. if, on the other hand, a philosophical decision were to be taken, or even amendment no 28 to the oomen-ruijten report, which calls for total rejection, were to be adopted, we would be in the grip of total schizophrenia. it is therefore necessary to agree on the complementarity of these two instruments and to approve both of them in the proposed version.
- mr president, the two excellent reports we are considering are the clearest demonstration of the need for serious institutional reform to integrate the union's powers in the field of judicial, criminal and police cooperation, which today belong to the so-called third pillar, into the community framework. this is the proposal which the european parliament has repeatedly made and which i hope will be adopted by the convention on the future of europe and, therefore, by the intergovernmental conference on the reform of the treaties. only in this way can we avoid unproductive disputes and institutional conflicts in the future and, above all, work effectively to protect the rights of citizens. it is easy to see that, without effective community action, some of these rights - such as the right to a high level of protection and improvement of the quality of the environment, a right enshrined in article 37 of the charter of fundamental rights of the union - are not adequately protected by the member states. none of the member states has ratified the 1998 council of europe convention on the protection of the environment through criminal law. the very many community environmental directives do not provide sufficient protection because of poor enforcement and frequent non-compliance in the absence of effective sanctions. the commission proposal for a directive requiring member states to provide for criminal sanctions, as supplemented by the useful amendments indicated in the oomen-ruijten report, deserves therefore our full support. although the commission, parliament and the council's own legal service have repeatedly stressed that environmental protection is a fundamental objective of the community, in accordance with articles 3 and 6 of the ec treaty, that the correct legal basis for the protection of the environment through criminal law is article 175 of the treaty and that community law takes precedence over union law, the council intends to adopt a framework decision on the same subject which not only supplements but also interferes with the proposal for a directive, limits its scope, reduces its scope and removes the matter from the co-decision procedure with the european parliament. the di lello report very appropriately argues that this framework decision should be consistent with the directive, awaiting its adoption and referring to it, without repeating the elements already covered by the directive and, if necessary, supplementing it. i hope that parliament will approve both reports and that everyone will consider whether it is appropriate to avoid such harmful contradictions in the future by achieving full community involvement in the third pillar.
mr president, a few remarks on the oostlander report. i also join in the thanks to the rapporteur, but i cannot ignore certain remarks on the right of asylum, a humanitarian principle which no civilian can disagree with, but which must be delimited within precise limits if we are to avoid the serious and objective risk of seeing it used for the purpose, which is certainly not to be shared, of facilitating the entry of illegal immigrants into the territory of the european union. the document in question states that it wants to avoid the movement of asylum seekers from one member state to another, but we have some doubts whether this objective can be achieved with minimum standards such as those contained in the proposal, also in view of the possibility given to the member states to grant better and more extensive facilities to asylum seekers. i would like to point out two limitations to the proposal. firstly, there are many cases which are expected to be brought before the courts for the granting or refusal of grants, housing, care, etc.; this means that an infinite number of subjects are included in the public assistance system, with legal positions that are required by the host state, which in many cases does not even recognize them for its own citizens. secondly, the principle of free movement from the territory of the applicant and his family members has a clear consequence: the more likely an asylum seeker is to obtain asylum, the more likely he or she is to try to lose track of himself or herself, thus increasing the number of hard-to-trace illegal migrants. the problems here are serious and concrete. in fact, many rules treat the applicant's position as if it were that of a person who has already been granted such status, for example by regulating access to non-short-term activities such as on-the-job training. in conclusion, action is needed to cut the document so that it does not become a hindrance rather than a directive for the concrete and effective protection of persons entitled to asylum. we fear that this could be an obstacle to the repression of illegal immigration, a serious and worrying phenomenon.

- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, after so many years of work towards an effective community patent, we must point out that some problems remain: the language regime, the role of national patent offices in relation to the european patent office and the judicial system. despite repeated calls from heads of state and government and from the various european councils, most recently the barcelona council, the situation is not coming to a head. we have had the same problems in the legal affairs committee with regard to the question of languages. after lengthy discussions, the committee opted for the language regime already tried in the case of the community trade mark, under which applications may be filed in any of the official languages of the community. however, the applicant should also indicate a second language, the so-called procedural language, from a list of five languages - english, french, german, italian and spanish - which he would accept to be used for the proceedings, in particular opposition, revocation or invalidity proceedings. if the application is in a language other than the five above, the office would arrange for its translation into the language of the proceedings indicated by the applicant. it is not, in my view, an ideal solution. for reasons of economy it would have been better to have only one language, english. this is also what european industry is asking for. however, this has not been possible, and so the alicante model is welcome, which is the only possible solution, although perhaps not the best. as regards the judicial system, the committee on legal affairs suggests a first instance court at national level, so that national courts with experience in patent litigation, such as the community patent courts, could be used, while the decision at second instance would be taken by the european intellectual property chamber. it is a compromise solution. we would have preferred a single, centralised court of first and second instance, which would have ensured greater uniformity of interpretation. but here too, opposition has been very strong. finally, the national patent offices are guaranteed to continue to play an important role in the procedures for granting the community patent. in conclusion, we do not think that the solution we have found is one hundred percent satisfactory, but we are finally closing this complex issue. i think that the rapporteur, mr palacio - to whom i naturally wish to congratulate on her work - shares these concerns. but in this procedure parliament is only consulted, it is not a co-legislator. we therefore give the green light, hoping that the council of ministers will be able to reach an agreement as soon as possible, without hiding behind any alibi.

mr president, as the rapporteur has very well explained, the purpose of this directive is not to discuss the dangers of asbestos, but to start from the certainty of this fact. although further scientific research is needed to fully clarify the lingering doubts about the dangers of asbestos to human health, the number of asbestos-related deaths in europe is such that a majority of member states have adopted a ban on the marketing and use of products containing asbestos. the problem today is also to take account of the shift in the risks associated with asbestos from one sector to another: the risks of asbestos are not limited to the traditional risks in the manufacturing sector - which, although significant, are controllable - but also to the risks in sectors where asbestos is handled in the context of removal, maintenance, repair and demolition work. the latter are potentially high and foreseeable risks for which it is essential to be guided by the precautionary principle in the definition of exposure limits. moreover, the risks associated with the use of asbestos do not only affect workers who are directly exposed to it, but also, to a lesser extent, the workers' family members and persons living near the construction sites. although, fortunately, italian legislation is more advanced than the proposed legislation, it is important today to support the rapporteur and to approve the report, because it is necessary to state, without ambiguity, that the level of safety at the workplace cannot be lowered. we must never forget that high competitiveness is also based on high social quality and that the quality of work is an important factor in production. in conclusion, beyond the general political considerations mentioned, which remain essential for us socialists, it should be remembered that the internationalisation of the economic and social costs of occupational diseases, ascertained or to be ascertained, and accidents at work, should make everyone understand, unequivocally, that the safety and health of workers, as well as being a right, is also a benefit for the undertakings themselves and for the economy in general. most of which are in africa - spend an average of 40 percent of their annual budgets on debt service, which reduces their ability to invest and thus to provide their populations with basic social services, such as health care and even education. paradoxically, the development aid that the european union and its member states provide to the world's poorest countries is sometimes not even enough to finance the servicing of their external debt. it should be added that the events of 11 september are having an impact on the situation at the moment, and by slowing down the global economic development, they are aggravating the already serious problem of these peoples. some figures: the debt of highly indebted countries rose from $147 billion in 1989 to $214 billion in 2001; today, 41 of the poorest countries on the planet are in a state of bankruptcy. 300 out of 600 hipc citizens survive on less than a dollar a day. i am not going to tell you anything about the lives of these people, who are suffering from diseases such as aids, tuberculosis and malaria, which are on the increase at the moment, and particularly about the situation of children, the disabled and the sick, since the elderly are not to be mentioned in these countries. the decision point has now been reached and 26 countries are now eligible for debt relief, which means that they can directly benefit from debt relief, but in order to officially benefit from debt relief by reaching the completion point - which is currently only reached by four countries - they must implement a pre-established package of social and structural reforms and maintain good macroeconomic performance. strangely, however, no date is set for reaching this completion point, although the average period should in reality be at least 15 months. this short time frame also leaves highly indebted countries little time to develop multi-sectoral poverty reduction strategies and requires local governments to spend money and funds to return to completion point rather than to tackle a sustainable and credible poverty reduction agenda. in general, however, we can say that the enhanced hipc initiative, while acknowledging the failure of previous programmes and experiences on macroeconomic strategies, is wholly insufficient on its own to solve this problem in the current context of economic globalisation and does not actually reduce the nominal debt of these countries. if the debt is not drastically reduced, these countries will be forced to pay it off indefinitely. the european parliament and the commission in particular have strongly supported the need to cancel this debt, also in the wake of the jubilee 2000 campaign in which various political, civil and religious organisations and movements - - madam president, although world wealth has increased eightfold since 1960, we must regrettably point out that today one in two people live on less than a dollar a day, one in five have no access to clean water, one in six are illiterate and one in three children suffer from malnutrition. these alarming figures are echoed by the united nations development programme and unicef, which have calculated, for example, that an annual expenditure of 80 billion dollars over a period of ten years could guarantee every human being access to basic education, basic medical care, adequate nutrition, access to clean water, sanitation, as well as access for women to gynaecological and obstetrical care: a sum four times less than what the third world pays back for its external debt, a quarter of the us military budget, 18 percent of the world's advertising expenditure, 9 percent of military spending, half the assets held by the four richest people in the world. these are data that should make us think. in 1999, developing countries repaid creditors in the nordic countries, according to world bank figures for 2000, $300 billion, the equivalent of four marshall plans. the european union is committed to ensuring that the debts of poor countries are reduced or cancelled. the beneficiary countries, for their part, should commit to good governance and to channelling the savings from debt reduction towards achieving equitable and sustainable development standards for their populations.

commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to thank mrs foster for her excellent work and the professionalism she has shown over the past few months. as you all know, less than a month had passed since the tragic events of 11 september and the commission was already proposing, with this initiative, to tighten up the safety requirements applicable to civil aviation in a harmonised way and, when this proposal was sent to parliament and the council, the urgency of reaching agreement on this was raised. parliament agreed with this urgency and acted accordingly, concentrating only on the operative part of the regulation and leaving aside the technical annex which was based on the work of a specialised body, the ecac (european civil aviation conference) and, in particular, on document no 30 on aviation safety from that organisation. now that the text has been analysed in greater detail, the commission understands that the transport committee of parliament is proposing 33 amendments to the common position. last week there was an attempt to reach a compromise on this issue between parliament, the council and the commission and, as mr jarzembowski and mrs foster have just said, unfortunately it was not possible to achieve it. the commission stresses the urgency of this document. if an interinstitutional dispute arises, i fear we could be faced with a dead end. i therefore call for and ask once again for a spirit of commitment on the part of both the council and parliament so that we can finally resolve this matter before the summer. i would like to stress what i have said on other occasions, namely that the commission will continue as usual to work towards agreements as mediators. as for the amendments, i would classify them into four categories. the first, which is aimed at making the rules on aviation safety stricter, is the one with the largest number of amendments and which we can accept in its entirety. in addition, amendment no 8, which calls for surprise airport inspections, is acceptable in principle. the aim is to ensure that airports are not warned of inspections, but the commission would like the inspection to be carried out with the knowledge and cooperation of the national regulatory authorities, as is the case with competition or agricultural inspections. in other words, the national regulatory authorities would be informed, but not the individual airports. we feel that would be the right balance. amendment no 16, which is supported by the commission, deserves special mention. it's the requirement that all personnel be screened when they enter secure areas. the commission agrees that airline staff should be subject to the same level of scrutiny as passengers and not to lower levels. recall that many terrorist incidents have occurred because of the lack of security inside airport facilities. the purpose of amendment no 20 by the rapporteur is to increase safety. in this case, the commission understands that it would make things very difficult without really bringing about any concrete results, and in that sense we must reject it. the commission generally rejects the amendments in the second package, which seek to reduce safety standards. these are amendments nos 6, 13, 17, 27, 30 and 31, and in particular amendments nos 6 and 13. the first is to increase the number of airports exempted from harmonised community rules by raising the size threshold for aircraft. as no indication has been given to the commission as to the number of additional airports which would be exempt from the regulation, if this amendment were adopted, we reject it as it would introduce a legally unknown situation. we also reject amendment no 13, which would delay the entry into force of certain elements of the regulation by 12 months, since all the safety rules in the regulation are based on standards adopted by the ecac, to which all the member states of the union belong. we believe that its application should not be delayed any further, but on the contrary, we understand, as mr jarzembowski said a moment ago, that it is urgent to apply the regulation as soon as possible. the third group of amendments aims to extend the scope of the regulation, and therefore explicitly establishes the obligation of the union states that the member states should finance and be responsible for the additional security measures. the commission supports these arguments - and i want to make this very clear - and in particular amendment no 7 on the fair financing of the additional security costs. but these amendments are not relevant to this regulation and are completely outside article 80 of the treaty, which is the legal basis of the treaty. moreover, if it were possible to include rules on additional funding in this regulation, they would not invalidate the higher community rules on state aid which remain applicable. the commission therefore formally rejects amendments nos 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10, 11 and 12, although it is prepared to examine the issues raised from a broader perspective, including the need for greater organisation in the area of financing of investments in aviation safety. if necessary, after a detailed study, it is prepared to submit a legislative proposal, but separately and not in the context of this regulation. finally, the commission considers all amendments aimed at improving the regulation from a grammatical point of view while maintaining its content to be fully acceptable. amendments nos 16, 19, 21 to 26, 28, 29, 32, 33 and 34 and amendments nos 14, 15 and 18 could therefore be accepted after some changes in wording. the commission and the european parliament generally share a very similar position in this field. we both believe that there is a need for good basic harmonised standards on civil aviation safety and that special emphasis should be placed on this regulation. the proposal, once adopted, will be a very important step towards ensuring a high level of aviation safety throughout the european union. parliament and in particular mrs foster, with her excellent work throughout this report, are making an important contribution to this result. what we need now is also a collaborative attitude on the part of the council and a compromise between all of us at the end that will allow us to move forward and avoid a deadlock on an issue that we must resolve as soon as possible.

- the next item is the recommendation for second reading (a5-0122/2002) by mrs berger, on behalf of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, on the common position adopted by the council with a view to adopting a directive of the european parliament and of the council on the distance marketing of financial services to consumers and amending council directives 90/619/eec, 98/27/ec and 98/27/ec (riv. 1 - c5-0697/2001 - 1998/0245 (cod)).
commission. – mr president, let me begin by confirming that the commission supports the council's common position and agreed with the original recommendation of your rapporteur, mrs berger, that parliament should adopt the common position without amendment. however, we support the compromise amendments proposed by mrs berger and mr lehne – amendments nos 43 and 44 – and urge parliament to adopt the common position with these amendments only. let me pause here to record my thanks to mrs berger for the hard work that she has done on this particular piece of legislation, and also to mr lehne, for their cooperation and hard work with both myself and my services. we believe that the common position constitutes a balanced solution which improves our amended proposal and, to a considerable extent, meets the wishes of parliament as expressed in its first reading. in particular, the common position includes: fully harmonised and detailed general information requirements; the principle of written confirmation; a right of withdrawal with some exceptions; protection for the user on the chosen means of payment and redress in the event of disputes. the directive complements and underpins the e-commerce directive by introducing an additional safety net of protection measures for consumers. this directive also fits into a larger framework of legislative measures designed to open up the internal market for retail financial services. allow me to comment on the 50 amendments tabled. let me begin by addressing amendments nos 9, 10, 11 and 37 that expressed members' concerns about the position of intermediaries in this directive. in the common position, the supplier is defined only as the "contractual provider", and this is deliberate. adding the concepts of "intermediary" and "agent" would require a precise outline of the operation of various categories of financial intermediaries and an exhaustive description of the relationship between suppliers and intermediaries or agents. as indicated by recital 19, this is not possible in the framework of a general and horizontal directive that applies to all financial services. i can confirm that the intervention of a contractual provider face-to-face implies that the transaction falls outside the scope of the directive. the directive applies to organised distance marketing schemes not to face-to-face schemes with the occasional distance transaction. i shall now address the amendments that are unacceptable because they attack the core of the common position. i shall begin by commenting on the alleged impact of article 3(4) on the e-commerce directive and, in particular, the principle of country of origin. i fully agree with the speech made by mrs berès on this particular point earlier. the commission firmly believes that the common position establishes rules that complement the e-commerce directive and fill gaps in it. among these, article 3(4) is central. amendment no 13 proposes deleting article 3(4). the amendment is, in my view, based on a misinterpretation of the article. article 3(4) provides indispensable clarification of an important aspect of the e-commerce directive. the article states that the information communicated to the consumer, prior to conclusion of the contract, needs to be consistent with the provisions which will be contained in the contract itself. this makes sense legally and in practice. contractual obligations are not subject to the country of origin approach, and article 3(4) simply refers to the law and i quote, "presumed to be applicable", normally meaning the law of the country of destination. no reputable supplier would willingly misinform consumers about the future content of their contract on the pretext that such information was subject to country of origin rather than country of destination rules. in addition, the article only covers the prior information which will eventually be reflected in the contract. it does not cover all the information provided before the contract is signed but not subsequently included in the contract itself. finally, the information contained in article 3 must be communicated and addressed personally to the consumer. situations where the supplier provides general information to an indefinite number of recipients are thus excluded. another concern is the wish to adopt a maximum level of harmonisation. amendment no 3 proposes the deletion of the content of recital 9; amendment no 5, a substantial change to recital 13. amendments nos 26, 27 and 28 provide for the deletion of article 4(2) to (4), and amendment no 25 a fundamental change to article 13. again, i must disagree with these proposed amendments. the implementation period for the e-commerce directive expired in january this year. once the distance selling directive has been adopted, there will still be a two-year implementation period. so for on-line transactions, the principle of country of origin will apply to generalised pre-contractual information for a time during which the provisions of this directive are being implemented. it would be extremely unhelpful for consumer confidence if this period were to be perceived as leading to, or effectively did lead to, the lowering of consumer protection standards in any one member state. to avoid this, recital 9 recalls that further convergence or harmonisation at a higher level of consumer protection is foreseen in a number of areas, as laid down in the financial services action plan. pending this harmonisation, there should be no lowering of standards. the deletion proposed by amendment no 5 would make the recital factually wrong. the directive in certain places, such as in article 10, leaves member states some leeway with the harmonised framework. article 4(2), introduces the possibility for member states to impose additional information requirements. the commission concluded from the inventory of information requirements it made in 2000, that this provision is inescapable. information requirements in the area of financial services are of a diverse and complex nature, they are regulated partly by ec law, partly for the time being by national law. much has been done at sectoral level to harmonise pre-contractual information requirements. however, it is clear that we are not yet in a position to base information obligations only on ec law. deletion of article 4(2), as proposed in amendment no 26 – although already rejected by the committee on legal affair and the internal market – would prevent member states from regulating information requirements, notably where no community legislation existed at all and would in effect roll back important national consumer protection rules. for this reason, pending further harmonisation, member states may maintain or introduce more stringent rules. however, the imposition of any additional rules must conform with the transparency procedure laid down in article 4(3), which has to be maintained, contrary to the suggestions made in amendments nos 27 and 28. amendment no 25 includes the deletion of the phrase at the end of article 13 "where those operators are in a position to do so". this phrase is found in the equivalent article in the general directive. it is not a minimal clause, it is a reflection of the situation on the ground in all member states. if it were to be deleted, postal service operators for instance could be obliged to breach mail secrecy. finally, it is an exaggerated concern for the level of harmonisation to seek to transform the directive into a regulation as required by amendment no 49 and to fix a date for end of transposition, even before the directive is adopted, as is suggested in article 50. amendments nos 6 and 8 carve out contracts concluded before a notary. the consequence would be that intervention of a notary in a distance contract on financial services would deprive the consumer of central rights laid down in the directive, and this is clearly unacceptable. these rights include information that only the supplier can give, for instance on the quality and risk of a product, protection in case of fraudulent use of cards and protection against unsolicited services and communications. the effect of a mandatory exclusion of a right of withdrawal for mortgage credit, as contained in amendments nos 20, 22, 30 and 32, and the suppression of a right of reflection – amendment no 31 – would be a substantial reduction of consumer protection in member states. furthermore, although the definition of mortgage credit found in amendment no 20 is the same as the definition in the code of conduct on home loan information negotiated between industry and consumers in 2001, national legislation goes beyond the latter definition. reduced consumer protection would also follow the suppression, through amendment no 42, of the optional exemption to the obligation to pay for insurance services and the limits introduced by amendment no 33. some amendments include provisions that are unacceptable simply because of their content. amendment no 12 seeks to introduce a specific definition of credit. i understand this is to solve a problem with the transposition in one member state of the general directive on distance contracts – directive 97/7/ec. any problems relating to the general directive should be resolved in that context and not in this legislation. amendment no 15 introduces a sunset provision: a deadline after which a consumer may no longer invoke the right of withdrawal. this would amount to punishing the consumer for disrespect of obligations by the supplier. amendment no 17 would exclude from the right of withdrawal contracts whose performance has begun with the consumer's consent, before the end of the withdrawal period. in the general directive on distance contracts (97/7/ec), the consumer loses his right of withdrawal. if he accepts that the performance of the contract begins. in contrast this directive foresees that if a consumer withdraws he must pay for services actually rendered before the withdrawal. amendment no 17 would render amendment no 7 meaningless. however, this would contradict the european parliament's position during first reading, when it voted in favour of the principles contained in this article. amendment no 23 on payment for services rendered confuses the respective obligations of consumers and suppliers. consumers must pay for services rendered if they withdraw. a good example is an insurance contract. suppliers must return any sums received before the consumer withdraws, for instance where the contract is for investments. i am not convinced of the need for amendments nos 24 and 48 on tacit renewal. the provision in article 1(2), on initial services agreements, followed by successive operations or a series of separate operations of the same nature, amply covers the concern that underlines that amendment. amendment no 35 makes the rules on burden of proof mandatory. this disregards the fact that the civil law of member states is not harmonised. article 46 removes the need to obtain the consumer's explicit consent to receive a shortened list of information requirements in telephone communications and replaces this by a reference to the rules on confirmation of information. this would lead to a substantial weakening of the consumer protection established by this directive. i have covered the most important amendments. the remaining amendments – nos 1, 2, 4, 7, 14, 29, 34, 36, 38 to 40, 45 and 47 – are either less precise than the common position or do nothing to improve it. there is an urgent need to fill the gap and establish the legal certainty that this directive would offer. the directive has been negotiated since 1998. if it fails, neither business nor consumers will be better off. i urge you to follow the lead of your rapporteur and other speakers who urge this, and adopt this directive without any further delay, only with the compromise amendments suggested. thank you for your attention.

- madam president, mr president-in-office of the council, mr commissioner, some three years after the tampere council, which defined a strategy for creating an area of freedom, security and justice in the union and laid the foundations for a work programme and a common policy on immigration and asylum, it is now possible to take stock of the progress made, or not made, and of the current state of affairs. i am sorry to say that the budget is neither positive nor encouraging. the commission, in implementing the tampere conclusions, has indicated, through a legislative programme, the need to develop a proactive policy, which recognises that the migratory pressure is bound to continue, that there are benefits that orderly immigration can bring to europe, to the immigrants themselves and to their countries of origin. the approach proposed by the commission indicates a comprehensive policy which addresses all the problems: the commission has also adopted a communication on the implementation of the european year of the environment, which sets out the main priorities for the european union in the field of environmental protection. all this, as we know and as you, mr president, have mentioned, means working simultaneously on five policies: the definition of legal channels for immigration; the fight against illegal immigration; fair treatment, based on the principles of non-discrimination against non-eu citizens and integration policies; partnership with countries of origin; the mission to europe for humanitarian reasons. despite this positive attitude on the part of the commission, supplemented by the contributions of parliament, the budget is neither positive nor encouraging. i believe that the council has a great responsibility in all this, because on the one hand it shows the way forward - it did so in tampere - and on the other hand it has consistently failed to fulfil its commitments and has not taken the responsibility that comes with them. the council and many governments forget that one of the causes of immigration is precisely the needs of our labour market. there is a failure to identify the needs of the labour market, the fight against undeclared work, the link between all this and a proper immigration policy. the emphasis is on security problems, which are real but which must be tackled with balance, with the basis of its policy being respect for the law and the rights of individuals. but when it comes to security and immigration, what characterizes some governments in europe, for example in italy, is a combination of alarmism and miraculousness. immigration is seen as a danger to be defended against, fears are fuelled and the problem is promised to disappear miraculously, demagogic slogans are used to suggest that everything is permissible to the forces of the state and the police to ensure order. on the contrary, a serious security policy is based on two interrelated pillars: to keep the doors open, within precise rules and limits, to legal immigration flows. i repeat: doors open, not wide open. the other pillar is to tackle illegal immigration effectively. but if the first fails, the second is strengthened, because the most desperate and determined - or forced - to emigrate throw themselves into the arms of criminal traffickers who offer to take them to europe in their death carts. if it is true that the concerns of the citizens cannot and must not be ignored, it is also true that they cannot be addressed, let alone resolved, on the basis of alarmism and blind repressive policies.

commission. - mr president, i am pleased to present to parliament this third report on public finances in economic and monetary union for the year 2002, which consists of an analytical report drawn up by the directorate-general for economic and financial affairs and a commission communication setting out the main conclusions of economic policy. one of the objectives of the report is to help ensure that the commission continues to play a leading role in the debate on budgetary policy in the union. the report provides a detailed overview of budgetary developments and prospects in the member states and in the euro area as a whole. it also provides important clarifications on the scope and methods of the budgetary surveillance process in the union, which allows for greater transparency in our assessment of the budgetary position of each member state. finally, it takes a forward-looking approach by presenting an analysis of some of the main budgetary challenges facing the union in the future. let me make a few brief comments on recent budgetary developments and their prospects, in which i shall refer to the main conclusions of the report. i will begin by highlighting some of the most important features of recent developments: 2001 was the most difficult period for fiscal policy in the history of economic and monetary policy. the budget deficit for the euro area reached 1.3% of gross domestic product, the first increase since 1993. despite this increase, given the decline in activity during this period, the budgetary behaviour can be considered acceptable. first, member states - especially those which had already reached budgetary equilibrium or surplus - were able to allow the automatic stabilisers to operate to offset the negative effects. secondly, in contrast to previous periods of declining activity, no country running a deficit engaged in unjustified expansionary policy. thirdly, member states have been able to pursue their planned tax reforms to remedy supply rigidities despite various complaints that the stability pact deprived the authorities of their freedom as a result of arbitrary or inflexible rules. in summary, i would say that fiscal policy has remained broadly neutral, allowing for a balanced economic policy favourable to growth and price stability. however, this positive assessment should be broadly qualified in the case of four countries: germany, france, italy and portugal, which are in deficit and do not meet the requirements of the stability and growth pact. in particular, the deficits of portugal and germany have increased to levels close to the 3% reference value, prompting the commission to activate the early warning mechanism. it is important to recognise, however, that the decline in economic activity has been neither too pronounced nor too long lasting, but, unless all member states achieve the medium-term objectives set out in their stability programmes, future declines in activity could pose a more serious test for the union's budgetary surveillance framework. the focus on the key issue of the last few months - early warning - has left out a number of important measures which, in my view, strengthen the quality and scope of budgetary surveillance. i would like to highlight three: firstly, a revised code of conduct on the content of the presentation of the stability and convergence programmes was adopted in 2001 and has already been applied to the current programmes, which has allowed the council to improve the evolution of the programmes and has also allowed us to know the aggregate effect of the budgetary objectives for the area of the european union as a whole. secondly, the commission and the council have developed a common method for calculating cyclically adjusted budgetary balances. the recent downturn in economic activity and the experience gained with the early warning mechanism have highlighted the importance of taking into account the underlying budgetary positions when assessing the budgetary situation of different member states. thirdly, we have carried out an analysis of the sustainability of public finances in the light of an ageing population and have included this assessment in the stability and convergence programmes. according to the barcelona european council, long-term sustainability will be a permanent objective in the budgetary surveillance procedure. i now wish to make a few comments on the recent experience of rapid alerting in accordance with the provisions of the pact: i have already explained on several previous occasions the reasons why the pact was put into effect, and i shall not dwell on that point today, but will merely make a few comments on subsequent developments. the council has decided, as you know, to close the rapid alert procedure, as the two countries concerned have reiterated their willingness to implement their stability programmes fully in order to avoid breaching the 3% of gross domestic product reference value and to resume the process of budgetary consolidation in order to achieve their medium-term objectives in 2004. it is clear that the authorities are taking these commitments seriously and i welcome the progress made in germany on an agreement between the länder and the central government on the control of public finances, which allows us to highlight the fact that the question of sound public finances is not a matter for the central government alone, but involves all levels of government. as regards the experience of this early warning system, my view is that it is necessary to distinguish between the procedure, which as you know proved difficult, and the results we have achieved so far, which can be considered positive. the commission, the council and parliament should take note of this first experience and draw some lessons which i think are important. firstly, with the new recovery coming, we believe it is essential to stress again the need to continue the process of budgetary consolidation in order to achieve the rule of proximity to balance or surplus so that we can deal with possible situations similar to those we have experienced in the past. secondly, we should remember that the budgetary problems that mainly affected the large euro area countries in 2001 and 2002 are the consequence of not having taken advantage of the opportunities offered by the period of high growth from 1998 to 2000. thirdly, as the report i refer to points out, automatic stabilisers should be the normal method of stabilising the economy, while discretionary measures should remain the exception. however, a clear agreement among economic policy makers in the union on the criteria for assessing discretionary fiscal policies would increase their transparency and predictability in budgetary behaviour. finally, member states should improve the compatibility between their internal budgetary rules and budgetary commitments within the union framework. it will now comment on the quality and sustainability of public finances in response to the lisbon strategy. significant improvements have been made in the sustainability of public finances. the commission and the council have assessed the sustainability of public finances on the basis of the medium-term budgetary objectives set out in the stability and convergence programmes. the analysis clearly shows that, with current policies, there is a risk of budgetary imbalances in some member states and these risks are multiplied in the case of countries that do not achieve the medium-term objectives set out in their stability and convergence programmes. this year's report also looks at the quality of public expenditure and the lack of a clear definition of the quality of public expenditure has made it difficult to have a debate on this issue at union level. the absence, in some cases, of comparable data on the purpose for which public resources are spent also constitutes a limitation for this debate. the report therefore simply seeks to open this debate on the quality of public spending by focusing on the composition of public spending and is itself consistent with the achievement of the objectives of the lisbon strategy, namely to increase growth and employment. this analysis suggests that most countries succeeded in improving the composition of their public expenditure during the 1990s, while maintaining the size of the public sector. however, before drawing definitive conclusions on the quality of public expenditure, further analysis is necessary, taking into account the specific objectives of the spending programmes, their design and their relations with other economic policy instruments, and we intend to undertake this task in the coming years. finally, the document also includes a reference to the budgetary challenges for the enlargement countries: once they have joined the european union, these countries will be fully subject to the community acquis on budgetary policy and will have to submit their convergence programmes. in interpreting their budgetary positions, it is essential to take appropriate account of their specific needs and circumstances. the budgetary surveillance process should also take into account that the candidate countries are undergoing major structural and institutional changes. the limitations arising from the fact that these countries are generally characterised by greater instability in their production levels than the union countries and are small open economies that rely heavily on foreign capital to finance their recovery processes must therefore be considered. in the process of preparing for accession, candidate countries are not asked to meet the nominal convergence criteria, but to meet the copenhagen criteria. the main concern during the pre-accession period is medium-term macroeconomic stability, rather than the achievement of particular budgetary objectives. the medium-term budgetary policy must also pursue a revenue and expenditure structure favourable to economic growth. finally, the emphasis on structural and institutional reform should not obscure the importance of sound fiscal policies. the vulnerability of the candidate countries to economic shocks and external constraints underlines the need for prudent policies in these countries.
the commission is aware of the fact that the european parliament has been involved in the negotiations on the maastricht treaty for a number of years. we are aware that private debt is raising specific problems in some countries of the union. and as regards public debt, our basic idea remains the same as always: to reduce public debt rapidly, especially in those countries where it is approaching levels equivalent to gross domestic product; to this end we establish specific programmes of primary surpluses which allow an accelerated reduction of public debt.
the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the report to which i refer has a specific chapter on cases where a budgetary and discretionary policy might be useful, and you will read in it that, in our view, it should be used only in very specific cases, affecting only one country and under limited conditions. of course investment helps growth and in that sense we have always regarded investment spending as more positive than some types of current spending. however, this does not mean that it justifies any overrun of the established objectives of the stability pact. so yes to investment, but within the framework of the stability pact.
- mr commissioner, you referred to the question of the ageing population and therefore to the question of social security. the lack of social security reforms in the main european countries is a drain on economic development, undermines public budgets and is a factor in inequality between generations. does he not think that, since these calls for social security reforms are being made year after year, month after month, but nothing is happening in the various countries, that it is necessary for the commission to come up with clearer statements, with clearer figures, with clearer commitments, also to inform public opinion of what is happening, of the risks that are being run from the point of view of social security and of the risks that we are continuing to pass on to the new generations? this is to prevent that in a year, two years, five years, we are here repeating the same things and nothing will happen.
mr president, i am referring in particular to mr marinos' report, which is certainly very good because it has managed to touch on all the issues of great economic importance which are relevant in modern and equipped societies. capital movements, migration flows, labour market and pension systems have been analysed with synthetic proposals for solutions. the european economic landscape is still dominated by the stability and growth pact, which has emerged victorious from the economic storm of recent months. after 9/11, few of us really believed that the parameters set by the pact could be met. today, however, skeptics - many of them at least - have admitted their error and have changed their minds. the member states which had some problems to forgive themselves, particularly germany and portugal, did their best to reconcile the uncertainties and to rearrange some parameters which were moving towards the thresholds of attention. the rapporteur, with great ability, covers all economic issues and the major events from lisbon to barcelona, touching on the major problems of the ever-growing number of elderly people, of economic refugees who, together with their families, represent for the host states a variable of uncertainty resulting from their absorption by the black labour market. paragraph 20 of the report certainly makes reference to the labour market, but the problem requires more and more rigorous analysis. the profit-sharing system, employee ownership, and the profit-related pay system - policy. the whole of america, from canada to the strait of magellan, is a continent on which the culture, history and life of europe have had a great deal of influence. the result of this involvement has been a hybrid society, different, non-european but based on the values that have been inherited from our centuries-long presence throughout this vast continent. the european union's aim is to value the idiosyncrasies and independence of all these countries, but at the same time to promote all those purely european values which are still alive in these societies and which we, through our policies, have an obligation to maintain. of course, we have to do more than that, and that is why we are so involved in the issue of economic development. but we also know that the solutions are always long-term, because there are areas, such as central america or the andean region, or even the most developed, the southern cone region, which, precisely because of the circumstances in which they find themselves, have practically mortgaged the coming years in a very serious way and with social consequences that can be extraordinarily dangerous for the future of these countries. i therefore believe that the examples that have been given, such as the free trade agreement with mexico and the one we are now going to be able to conclude with chile, establish a path to a fairer and in writing. - (it) the european research area is a reality in the making: it is an ambitious objective of the european union which, through the sixth framework programme, aims to coordinate research activities in such a way as to enable europe to compete with the other major world nations in the field of science and technology. the actions undertaken under the sixth framework programme for research and technological development 2002-06 will be implemented, for the first time, in accordance with the general objectives for research set out in the ec treaty, which are aimed at: - strengthening the scientific and technological bases of industry and the community; - promoting the development of the competitiveness of industry and the community; - promoting research actions consistent with the principles of the treaty on european union. the research priority themes proposed in the sixth framework programme were defined on the basis of the 'european added value' criteria which are based on: - the desire to gather and concentrate a critical mass of financial and human resources while limiting dispersion as much as possible; - the need to combine the different complementary skills present in the different countries of the union and to use comparative studies at european level; - the creation of links with the priorities and interests of the union; - the necessarily transnational nature of research. these traditions - summarised in the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. like any solution that must balance different interests, it must be evaluated as a whole. it seems to me reasonable and sustainable, since the european parliament certainly does not have the power to get the council to prevent member states from retaining traffic data for reasons of national security. we can 't stop it . we can provide a framework of guarantees, of certainties and of protection of fundamental rights so that future legislation must respect them.

concessions to accommodate those in parliament not in favour of a harmonised policy. amendments nos 9, 18, 28, 44 and 45 are acceptable, both for the council and the commission. the exception clause and directly enforceable. as we have said from the start of the discussions, the directive we are debating today is not a third pillar instrument. it imposes legal limitations on what we can usefully include in the provisions of the directive, both with regard to any national measures for public security or crime-fighting and with regard to safeguarding individual rights and freedoms. as the commission has emphasised in its recent submission to the european convention, we think that the separation between the three pillars causes numerous difficulties and should therefore be abandoned. but as long as the pillars exist, we are forced to respect them, because the european court of justice would not uphold any third pillar elements included in a first pillar directive. for similar reasons, we cannot introduce a provision on the cost of law enforcement measures in this directive, as proposed in amendment no 39. nevertheless, i can assure mrs cederschiöld that the commission will requested split vote, the whole compromise would unravel and this would surely lead to conciliation with an even more uncertain outcome. the commission understands the concerns that have motivated the opt-in for solicited commercial e-mail, similar issues are at stake for proposed harmonised opt-in regarding directories. a non-harmonised solution as proposed in amendment no 35 is not sustainable with the internal market. in summary, an agreed overall solution between all institutions is within reach if the european parliament tomorrow accepts amendments nos 9, 13, 18, 25, 26, 28, 37, 38 and 44 to 50. the result will be a directive with great added value for european citizens and for the development of the information society.

- the next item is the recommendation for second reading (a5-0136/2002) on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on the common position adopted by the council with a view to adopting a directive of the european parliament and of the council on public access to environmental information and repealing council directive 93/313/ec (rapporteur: mrs korhola).
the commission. mr president, i would like to thank you. i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. environmental issues are best handled when all concerned citizens participate at the appropriate level. this important principle came directly from principle 10 of the rio declaration, which puts citizens at the centre of environmental policy. without access to environmental information, it is difficult for them to participate, which is why this proposal is so important. in 1998, the member states of the european community signed the unece convention on access to information, public participation in decision-making and right of appeal in environmental matters, known as the aarhus convention. this convention is a major step forward in implementing principle 10 of the rio declaration and continuing the process of transparency initiated by council directive 90/313/eec on the right of access to environmental information. i personally think it is very important that the community ratifies the convention as soon as possible. however, before this can be done, the community acquis must be brought into line with the provisions of the convention, and this is also one of the main aims of the proposal. thanks to the work of the rapporteur - and i thank mr korhola - the european parliament and the council, the proposal has been greatly improved in recent months. most of the amendments tabled by the european parliament reinstate amendments which the commission did not accept at first reading and which are intended to strengthen the commission's proposal. while i understand and respect your desire to maximise the public benefit of the proposal, i believe that some of the amendments impose obligations on member states which are unnecessarily burdensome and go beyond the aarhus convention. other amendments lay down in great detail the practical arrangements for providing information, whereas the proposed directive aims to provide a framework within which member states can adapt the rules to suit their own circumstances. we believe that the commission's proposal is well balanced. it covers the main obligations of the aarhus convention and more, and gives member states sufficient flexibility to implement legislation effectively. the commission can accept amendments nos 22, 28, 30, 32, 33, 42, 45 and 46 in their entirety. the commission can accept amendments nos 1 to 3, 9 to 1, 27 to 3 and 48 to 2 in part. the commission can in principle accept amendments nos 9 to 2, 19 and 27 to 2 after recasting or restructuring. the remaining amendments cannot be accepted by the commission, namely amendments nos 1 to 6, 7 to part 1 and part 2, 8, 10 to 18, 20, 21, 23 to 26, 27 to part 1, 29, 31, 34 to 41, 43, 44, 47 and 48 with the exception of part 2.
