- mr president, two points have always formed the basis of the european parliament's doctrine on immunities, even in the confused and difficult situation of interpretation, given the absence of a clear statute for a member of the european parliament: the first is that immunity does not protect the member but parliament. the second is that the european parliament must not in any way claim the right to judge the merits of matters, turning into a sort of court. i think - and frankly i regret to say it - that on both these points the duff report is innovating in a negative and dangerous way: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial interests are protected. in a situation where we are asking europeans to accept measures such as the european arrest warrant, and therefore to accept being arrested on the basis of evidence and procedures in force in a state other than our own, it seems to me really bizarre to allow any member to de facto block the judicial process. it is said that the member's right to act should be limited to cases of non-unionization, as referred to in article 9, and that then the committee responsible of parliament will be able to judge whether or not the member's request is acceptable. but in mr duff's text there is no such distinction between article 9 and article 10, and frankly, the fact that the committee responsible may be able to take a decision does not reassure me. the vote on immunity in the case of mr dell'utri, a man who was not even a member of parliament at the time, cannot reassure me because the votes of a parliament are always political votes. the procedure is therefore too complicated, leaving the door open to completely unprejudiced behaviour: i am sure that the commission will be able to take account of this in the future. that is why i shall be voting against the duff report, and i shall be asking my group to vote against it.
- mr president, the autonomy and independence of the european parliament, to which my colleagues have referred, are two of the principles on which the democratic legitimacy of the european union system is based. they must therefore be protected - and it is our duty - against attempts from various quarters to influence the exercise of parliamentary office. through the institutions of immunity and immunity from legal proceedings, provided for in the protocol on the privileges and immunities of the european communities, the european parliament has the means, even if partial, to defend itself against attacks on its independence or autonomy which may come from other public or private powers. this is not the case for the members of the european parliament elected in italy. the judicial authorities very often disregard the impeachable character of members of parliament - this must be clear to the european parliament - when they carry out the procedural acts provided for in article 68 (2) of the constitution, particularly in relation to telephone interception, even if this is done indirectly. in these very days there is a controversy in italy about these indirect telephone interceptions which have been made in defiance of the principle of this guarantee. it also indicates that in italy there is a confrontation, sometimes indeed with harsh tones, between the parliament and certain magistrates, who use their function by inevitably, and sometimes unknowingly, acting as a party. they are shielding themselves from the independence and institutional irresponsibility they enjoy by actually carrying out political actions. on the other hand, it is the magistrates themselves who theorize this role in conferences and seminars but also in official agendas. in the face of italy's peculiarity, the european parliament must vigorously defend its independence, especially when its members are accused of crimes for opinions expressed in the exercise of their functions. in concrete terms, the european parliament must be able to intervene to confirm cases of immunity from prosecution, even if the member who is subject to the procedure has been informed, if it is clear that there are conditions and prerequisites for the defence of its prerogatives, as the italian parliament does. the reports by mr maccormick and mr duff set out the procedures for giving effect to these guarantees. in conclusion, i thank both mr maccormick and mr duff for having set out in their report on the approval of the statute for members what we have written in this statute and i hope that it will be adopted as soon as possible in this house. the maccormick report, as approved by the committee on legal affairs, already takes a position on some of the cases reported and considers that those of colleagues or former colleagues marras, speroni and dell'utri are prima facie and in this case covered by non-unionism. in any event, the competent court - the italian court, in other words - must provide parliament with the documentation necessary to establish whether the case in question falls within the scope of the unenforceability hypotheses provided for in article 9 of the protocol. on behalf of the ppe-de group i cannot but fully share this approach and recommend that the reports by mr maccormick and mr duff be adopted without amendment, and i thank them for the excellent work they have done.
mr president, like mr corbett, i too share the approach taken by our rapporteurs, mr duff and mr maccormick, to the problems of the procedures for examining the immunity of members of the european parliament. the european parliament must in future have its own system of immunity, guaranteeing equal treatment to all its members, without distinction on grounds of nationality. and that can be one of the many tasks of the convention on the future of europe. but in the meantime, it is necessary to resolve some of the issues that have arisen in this parliament, particularly in the case of the spanish inquiry into mr berlusconi and others. in that case, the interpretation of the rules of procedure given by the president of parliament meant that the request, originating from the spanish judicial authority, was considered unsuitable and therefore never referred to the committee responsible, never examined by the european parliament until the main person concerned had left office as a member. in this case the request was considered to be from a foreign authority, to be transmitted through the government and its diplomatic representations. but in the european community the judicial authority of the member states cannot be considered as the authority of a foreign country, represented exclusively by its government. the proposal to amend rule 6 of the rules of procedure to require that parliament be informed immediately and that any request for immunity or waiver of immunity from any competent authority in the member states be referred to the committee responsible is therefore justified. the question raised in the maccormick report also arose in connection with cases involving italian members of parliament. article 9 of the protocol on privileges and immunities provides that, as in any democratic country, members of the european parliament may not be prosecuted for opinions expressed in the exercise of their functions. this is not a relative immunity which parliament can revoke, but absolute immunity from prosecution. it is provided for in a european law, which the courts of the member states are responsible for interpreting and applying. but in italy the practice has arisen that national members may invoke the protection of parliament in cases where they consider that their privilege has been unjustly denied or misinterpreted, and it was therefore considered that, by analogy with the provisions of article 10 of the protocol, this national practice should also be adopted at european level. this interpretation is now taken up in the duff report as a general solution and it is therefore proposed to amend the rules of procedure in such a way as to allow members to ask for the defence of their immunities and privileges, thus extending the possibilities of protection. the agreement to these proposals is an act of confidence in the dignity of politics, in its ability and willingness to guarantee democracy in the general interest and not to maintain the privileges of some against the principle of equality for all citizens. it is a confidence which i am determined to maintain, even if it is all too often disappointed, as is shown by one of the specific proposals in the report of the committee on legal affairs and citizens' rights, which says that these are opinions expressed in the exercise of office, even those expressed by mr dell'utri before he became a member of parliament. i therefore announce my vote in favour of the amendment proposed by mr maccormick.

the rapporteur. mr president, i should like to express my deep satisfaction at the adoption by the commission on 23 april of the directive on blood quality and safety standards, without there being any substantial departure from the position and amendments tabled by parliament. i believe that a directive can finally be adopted at second reading which offers the highest guarantees, especially for the benefit of patients and consumers, as regards the quality and safety of blood and its components, in order to avoid infections and complications which have been the subject of so many scandals and disasters in the past. the adoption of a new european directive, which provides for the same blood quality standards, will finally allow the free circulation of blood and its components in all countries of the european union and the disappearance of unwanted restrictions on the movement of donors from one country to another. high quality and safety standards will have to be applied at all stages of the transfusion process, from the collection of the blood from the donor to the control by specific and up-to-date laboratory tests, to the collection, processing, storage, distribution and use of whole human blood and its components. as you will no doubt remember, the most critical and controversial point in the directive in our committee and in the house concerned the so-called 'unpaid voluntary donations'. the common position adopted by the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection on this matter, in my view, settles all the disputes. article 4 of the treaty, which is based on the principle of subsidiarity, states: 'member states may introduce even stricter rules to ensure that donations are all on a voluntary and unpaid basis'; in addition, 'member states may restrict or prohibit the importation of blood and blood components from donors for payment'. in the committee on the environment and health the phrase was originally deleted: 'provided that the provisions of article 30 of the treaty are complied with'. today there is a new amendment tabled by the socialists, according to which all member states may prohibit or restrict imports of blood and blood components in order to ensure a high level of health protection and in order to achieve the objectives set out in article 19 (1), provided that the conditions of the treaty are met: i think it's a good compromise that can be sustained. the common position lays down specific provisions in article 19 concerning voluntary unpaid donations. in particular, in paragraph 1, member states shall encourage voluntary and unpaid donations and ensure that blood is, as far as possible, supplied through such donations. i think that is a very balanced provision and that position has already been adopted in the commission. article 19 (2) states, in a general way, that the member states shall inform the other member states and the commission of the measures taken to achieve the objective set out in paragraph 1. i would like to table an oral amendment to this effect, according to which this information, instead of being provided every two years, should be provided by the member states every three years, because this is in line with what is stated in a subsequent article. in addition, with regard to voluntary and unpaid donations, some colleagues have asked for the council of europe's definition to be introduced in the article and in particular in article 3. in principle i agree with the council of europe definition, but i think it is sufficient that it is referred to in recital 23, exactly as it is worded, which states that this definition 'should' - not 'must' - be taken into account by the member states. i am therefore opposed to amendment no 7 and amendment no 19, which seek to introduce the definition of 'voluntary unpaid donation' in a literal and rigid way. i think that a certain amount of flexibility is necessary in order to encourage donors. the commissioner, each member state has a different sensibility, traditions and culture on the definition of 'non-payment' which, in my view, must be respected. it is not for europe to impose strict definition criteria on individual member states. the fundamental thing, what is it? it is to have enough donors to achieve the most important goal, which is not to have a blood shortage, a shortage of blood and its components. another controversial point concerns the person responsible. i think that, with a compromise amendment, it should be left to the individual member states, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, to decide what kind of qualifications the person responsible must have. i hope, in conclusion, that this directive will finally see the light of day and be adopted.

commission. – mr president, as mentioned here by many speakers, with 9 000 pedestrians and cyclists killed and a further 200 000 injured in accidents involving a car, pedestrian protection has become a pressing concern for civil society, which the commission fully shares. when considering which approach to take to this issue, the choice has been between a voluntary commitment from industry on the basis of agreed objectives and the traditional route of legislation. after talks with the european commission, european motor vehicle manufacturers, represented by acea, committed themselves in june last year to introducing a range of measures starting this year, actually in january 2002, leading to a high level of pedestrian protection. identical commitments have been entered into since then by the japanese and korean automobile manufacturers. in a communication adopted in july last year, the commission presented to the european parliament and the council the main elements of the industry’s commitment and invited both institutions to express their views on it. the commission would decide thereafter whether to accept the industry commitment or to propose legislation. the commitment constitutes an innovative package that combines passive and active safety. on the passive safety side, manufacturers have agreed to design cars according to a series of tests introduced in two phases, starting in 2005, aimed at verifying that the car design will minimise injuries to pedestrians involved in an accident. another important passive safety element of the commitment is the ban of rigid bullbars from new cars as from this year. regarding active safety, industry has taken three additional initiatives: firstly, to equip new vehicles with abs from 2003 onwards, secondly, to introduce daytime running lights on all vehicles from 2002 (it should be noted that this refers only to the technical prescription of drl, but it does not supersede national laws on the use of drl), and, last but not least, industry is committed to progress and report systematically on the introduction of additional active safety devices to improve pedestrian protection, such as adaptive speed limiting devices. the commission would monitor the implementation of the commitment, on the basis of tests conducted by independent laboratories and possibly with the involvement of national type-approval authorities. since then, an intensive debate has taken place in the european parliament and the council in the past few months on the options presented by the commission in its communication. last november the council of ministers approved the idea of an industry commitment in this area and its fundamental elements, subject to certain conditions on particular points. now it is the turn of the european parliament to express its views. i am grateful to the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism and in particular to the rapporteur, mrs hedkvist petersen, for her impressive work, and also to mrs oomen-ruijten, mr harbour and mr rübig for their opinions. i appreciate the efforts invested in this matter, which have shown exceptional commitment, professionalism and openmindedness. the aim has been to seek a balance between a high level of protection, flexibility and efficiency in law-making on the one hand, and the preservation of legal certainty and transparency on the other. firstly, the commission welcomes the support expressed by the transport committee for the objectives and timeframe proposed in the commission communication for the introduction of pedestrian protection measures. secondly, the commission welcomes the views expressed in the report regarding the legislative approach, suggesting the use of framework legislation in this area to ensure legal certainty on the fundamental goals. it has been asked what the commission will do if the report is accepted. if a majority of the european parliament agrees to this approach, the commission is willing to put forward a proposal for framework legislation, based on the relevant measures of the commitment. i believe that we can do this by the end of the year, this coming autumn.

the rapporteur. - mr president, the transeuropean networks are one of the engines of growth in competitiveness and employment within our european union. the essen european council in december 1994 gave them a decisive political impetus by adopting a list of 14 priority projects. a number of financial instruments have been developed by the community and the european investment bank to achieve these objectives. the main objective of community assistance to tens is to help overcome the financial obstacles which may arise when a project is launched. at present, in principle, community assistance is limited to 10% of the overall costs, with the exception of the galileo programme which may receive up to 20% of its funding from the community. the remainder of the expenditure is to be co-financed through local, regional and national budgets. unfortunately, the work is not progressing as quickly as expected: of the 14 specific projects approved at the essen summit, only three were completed; six others are expected to be concluded by 2005; finally, as regards the other five, no clear indication was given as to their timetable. what are the problems then? firstly, the pace of investment has been too slow, and the commission considers that if the funding rate does not increase between now and 2010, it will be extremely unlikely to complete the network, in particular as regards the railway component. the biggest delays are in crossborder projects, as member states have given priority in their decisions to funding the local portions of the transeuropean network. these delays can be attributed mainly to the lack of an integrated approach to planning, evaluating and financing cross-border infrastructure. the community's financial resources and legal instruments do not allow it to act independently to accelerate such projects, since under the treaty national authorities are competent to implement a project on the territory of a member state. the areas most seriously affected by the persistence of bottlenecks are international corridors, where north-south traffic is highly concentrated, natural barriers such as the alps and the pyrenees, the periphery of major urban and commercial centres, where regional and local long-distance traffic meets and is concentrated, and some borders of the european union, in particular those with the candidate countries. the commission therefore proposes that community activities and projects should focus on reducing these bottlenecks. as regards implementation, the commission has been able to maintain a relatively high level of implementation in recent years and delays have been decreasing since 2002. the commission has therefore proposed to amend the general conditions for granting community financial aid in the tens sector. the aid would be increased from 10 to 20%, so as to have a multiplier effect and to attract mainly private investors. this amendment would concern three categories of projects: cross-border railway projects crossing natural barriers such as the alps or the pyrenees; projects to eliminate clearly identified bottlenecks at the borders with the candidate countries; the 12 priority projects in the energy sector. the first two categories fall within the scope of the ten-transport, as defined in decision 1692 of 1996. an additional amount of eur 100 million would be entered in the budget line for the transport tens - b5-700 - over the period 2003-06 to complement the support provided through ispa. the financial allocation for the tens and the financial perspective 2000-06 should therefore be reviewed. finally, the commission proposes to reallocate eur 50 million for crossborder projects under the current tens transport allocation. as regards galileo, its co-financing rate remains at 20%, as it was before. what are my observations? amendments nos 1, 3, 5 and 6 set the general framework by rebalancing the commission's presentation, which in its proposal tended to emphasize only the importance of projects involving the applicant countries. amendment no 2 calls on the commission to draw up an assessment of the responsibilities of the member states; amendment no 4 introduces the possibility for member states to use private capital if they consider it useful and stresses that, in the selection of projects, their economic and social added value and their compatibility with the objective of sustainable mobility must also be assessed; amendment no 7 states that the increase in the financial allocation is compatible with the financial perspective without causing cuts in other programmes. i would ask the commission to consult the budgetary authority again before reallocating funds under the transport tens. amendment no 8 - ten-transport - sets out the implementation of the network proposal as provided for in decision 1692/96, approved on 23 july '96; amendment no 9 authorizes the commission to recover sums granted for projects not completed within 10 years. amendment no 10 concerns the comitology and, finally, amendment no 11 concerns the so-called sunset clause. i hope that my presentation, although brief for time constraints, will be comprehensive, and i hope that we can complete the development of the tens, not only for ourselves but above all for the future of europe.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the rapporteur, mr turchi, and the committee on budgets have done a very good job, i think, of supplementing the commission's proposal in such a way as to make it more suitable for dealing with the main problem we have had, namely excessive delay. the innovations mentioned by mr turchi, from the extension of co-financing to 20 per cent to the provision of a time limit of ten years for completing the works, must be read in this light. i also think it is important to have included the galileo project and the telecommunications and energy network projects in the new regulation, and to have reiterated that the priority sector, also for sustainability purposes, is the railway sector. the positive work that has been done, however, leaves unchanged the need for a broader review of both the philosophy and the mechanisms of operation of the whole complex operation "networks". with the revision of cohesion policy and the enlargement of the union, the transeuropean networks are very closely related. on these three challenges, we socialists call for a great debate involving everyone and addressing the issue of networks in its true mission, which is to reduce inequalities within the union and to prevent what is becoming stronger, namely an enlarged union, from being a europe with a great engine that pushes forward, northern europe, and a heavy wagon that pulls away, namely southern europe.

the rapporteur. - ladies and gentlemen, today's report, which was adopted at the beginning of the year by the committee on budgets, is aimed at strengthening the powers of monitoring the budget of the european union during its implementation. the committee on budgets' report is intended to ensure that parliament's institutional role in adopting the european budget, which is a task entrusted to it by the treaties, is respected by ensuring that the budget adopted is consistent with the financial implementation. this is a necessary condition for the political priorities which parliament sets out annually in the financial document to be respected, a condition which the commission sometimes tends to forget. the committee on budgets had two objectives: the commission is also proposing to take stock of the situation in the first half of the year in order to identify the first signs of deviation from the budget as voted and to indicate to the committee the guidelines for the second half of the year. the fact that the own resources ceiling was not increased during the period of application of the financial perspective 2000-06 makes it all the more necessary to achieve these objectives, which will improve the quality of expenditure. in this context, parliament's monitoring of the situation highlights two types of problems: the commission has also been concerned about the excessive and sometimes improper use of financial flexibility instruments and the poor level of implementation of certain headings. to get a quantitative idea of what we are dealing with, it is enough to consider that, in the current financial year alone, the commission has already submitted transfers for a total volume of eur 250 million and that, for example, during the 2001 budgetary procedure, over 2 billion payment appropriations were transferred by means of transfers. to improve this situation, the commission is presenting, as from this year, a programme of implementation. this new instrument, which parliament has requested in agreement with the council, will allow for a more precise control of the situation, although it is not yet perfect. we believe that the commission should present this programming at the same time as it submits the requests to the budgetary authority and that it should also present this information in a more disaggregated form. in short, to ensure a closer and more systematic link with the appropriations initially voted, any request for transfer should take account of the budget voted, the actual implementation, the implementation profiles presented by the commission, a timetable for the implementation of the balance remaining on the line of origin and the analyses carried out by our parliamentary committees. if this information is not considered satisfactory, the transfer shall be rejected. in principle, therefore, requests for transfers which reduce the budget lines voted by parliament will not be accepted. the supplementary and amending budgets, on the other hand, raise a different kind of problem and make it possible to deal with unforeseen situations or to make the necessary adjustments to the budget following the closure of the accounts for the previous financial year. it was thanks to brs 1 that a solution was found for the financing of the convention; brs 2 and brs 3 - which will be discussed today - have in practice returned to the member states a total of almost eur 14 billion in payment appropriations not settled in the previous financial year. in order to improve the performance and image of the european union, this report calls on the commission to present a plan indicating the timetable for cancelled 2001 payments, to provide by 30 september a serious assessment of the state of payments for 2002, to accelerate or decommit payments of old commitments, including by cancelling outdated commitment appropriations. at present, the commission expects a rate of implementation at the end of the year of 100% for commitments and 97% for payments. in 2001 this was only 72 per cent, and if these results are achieved, we will have made real progress. as for the next brs, certainly the reconstruction of afghanistan and probably the middle east issue could require additional resources. the additional appropriations for reconstruction in afghanistan will only be used if the commission can demonstrate that the appropriations already entered in the budget have been correctly spent, also taking into account the commitments of other donors. as you can see, ladies and gentlemen, this is a report which is technical in some respects, but which shows how necessary it is that all the committees of our parliament should be involved in the control of the executive. i would like to say that in recent months, thanks to the excellent cooperation of all the budget rapporteurs from the various committees and together with mr färm, we have set up several monitoring groups for the various policies. if the situation improves, it will be partly thanks to the sometimes obscure efforts of the rapporteurs on the budget. parliamentary committees will thus be able to make parliament's democratic control over the commission even more effective in the future. i would remind you that, as of 15 june, the outstanding payments amounted to over eur 111 billion, which is more than the annual budget of the european union. although this is the natural distribution of payments over time, the commission must continue to reduce the burden of the past. the cancellation of 97 million of old commitment appropriations is a step in the right direction, albeit a timid one. finally, i would like to remind you that while cooperation with the commission has certainly been fruitful in recent months, we will probably have to converge on common action to achieve a result that is more in line with what the budgetary authority voted for at the beginning of the year.

- mr president, we are not all against gmos and their use. we are in favour of their regulated use, as the world situation demands: 50 million hectares of land worldwide are cultivated with gmos, compared with only 12 000 in europe. this should call into question the state of research at european level, as well as europe's role in the wto and the often discretionary and uncontrolled use of products containing gmos in developing countries. it should also call into question the value of safeguarding biodiversity and the meaning of guaranteeing consumer safety, which science is not yet able to guarantee with certainty. but this is not the time to do so. what is puzzling, however, in the proposals under consideration and in the subsequent work of the rapporteurs, is sometimes the way in which the principles of the cartagena protocol are translated. it seems that the precautionary principle and transparency, which are the basic elements of that protocol, are to be interpreted in a way that is sometimes even distorted, especially if one reads the second regulation, the one on traceability and labelling. there is no record of a method which, in a standardised way, certifies that operators have taken all the measures necessary to avoid contamination, nor is there any provision for an authority to certify that such measures have been used, nor is there any harmony between the permitted amounts of contamination. the same applies to samples to be submitted with the application for authorization, where the sampling is left to the discretion of the applicants for authorization. it is also not appropriate to place the burden of proving the quality of scientific analyses on economic operators, which is a subjective matter, since the cartagena protocol does not deal with the question of liability in any significant way either, and the examination of concepts is postponed until four years after the entry into force of the protocol. again , please . if the objective is traceability, in the light of the precautionary principle, it is not clear why an authorization granted must be valid for 10 years under one regulation, whereas the supporting documentation, under the other regulation, must be kept for only five years. the hope, in the work of the other rapporteurs and especially that of mrs scheele, who has also improved the commission's proposal, is that these points of perplexity will be corrected in order to find at least functional consistency.
- mr president, the orientation prevailing in the committee on the environment, thanks above all to the excellent work of our rapporteur, reinforces the particularly strict traceability and labelling system proposed by the commission. the primary duty of the union is to ensure maximum safety along all the different links in the production and distribution chain and to provide correct information on food on the market. it is then up to the consumer to choose whether or not to buy genetically modified food. this freedom of choice, however, presupposes a rigorous and reliable system of labelling, indicating whether products contain genetically modified organisms, are made of them, but also whether they are produced from them or with their help. the attempt by the people's party to re-propose in plenary the approach already adopted in the committee on the environment must therefore be firmly rejected. the commission's approach would be to reverse the approach and limit itself to the labelling of food or feed containing genetically modified dna or proteins, which would pave the way for a kind of colonization of the european agri-food system. the commission has not yet adopted a proposal for a directive on the protection of consumers in the event of accidents at work. the commission has also been very active in the fight against fraud, and i think that is a very important point. it may sound like an exaggeration, but tomorrow's vote is an important one for europeans: on the one hand, we can and must help them to overcome their insecurities; the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for approval.
- madam president, it is obvious that we are absolutely in favour of the adoption of regulations which ensure a high level of protection and safety for consumers and the environment, but we are also in favour of measures which are applied in a certain and transparent manner, and one of these measures is certainly labelling, which we believe should be implemented with a scientifically verifiable control system. while i thank the two rapporteurs for the enormous work they have done on such a difficult and complex subject, i must say that there are aspects of the two reports which raise certain questions: for example, the arbitrary lowering to 0.5% of the tolerance threshold, previously set at 1%, for the accidental presence of genetically modified materials; for example, what we consider to be an additional complication of the authorisation procedure without any improvement in safety or other benefits for the consumer. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's foodstuffs are not contaminated by genetically modified organisms. i would like to make a comment on the concept of "accidental presence", which is used to indicate the unintentional presence of small amounts of a certain atypical material in other material. well, when we are dealing with agriculture - which is, as always, a special sector - in the case of cultivated plant varieties, plants or propagating material, the accidental presence of traces of other varieties can occur at any stage of sowing, harvesting, transport, distribution; in some cases, accidental presence may also occur as a result of pollen exchange between varieties grown in neighbouring fields. now, in normal agricultural practice we are in a situation where point 9 of the proposal is placing us in objective difficulty. it would be important to avoid thresholds which do not take account of the facts.
the rapporteur. - madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the tragic accidents which have recently affected the chemical industry, but above all the people living around these sites and the environment, have been drawing the attention of the european union. baia mare, aznalcollár, but above all toulouse and enschede have become synonymous with human and environmental tragedies which we cannot leave without a clear response. it is in this delicate context that the commission has presented to parliament and the council its proposal to amend directive 96/82 of 9 december 1996 laying down the rules for the control of major-accident hazards involving certain dangerous substances, better known as 'seveso ii'. this proposal is the result of a thorough scientific work. we must therefore acknowledge the commission's willingness to address the weaknesses of directive 96/82 in a constructive spirit, which today allows us to send a clear message to both the chemical industry and the public. we will make every effort to ensure that appropriate control measures are adopted and respected. as rapporteur, i have tried to give priority to a methodological approach based both on the scientific basis of the proposed changes and on an assessment of the impact they will have on the european economic system. the introduction or strengthening of precautionary rules is certainly not easy. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the safety of the chemical industry is not compromised. the method for identifying the necessary changes is clear: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the safety of the road is not compromised. in practice, the proposal amends two basic types of criteria: minimum thresholds for the presence of substances at sites and the inclusion or reclassification of new activities or hazardous substances, in order to strengthen controls and the prevention of accidents. this will of course lead to a considerable increase in the number of sites covered by the new directive, but it must not be forgotten that public safety and the protection of the environment from substances capable of causing irreversible damage are at stake. i shall therefore use this methodology to present briefly the substantive changes proposed by the commission and the amendments proposed by our parliament. the incidents at baia mare in romania and aznalcollár in spain prompted the commission to include mining and landfilling in the scope of the directive. the committee on the environment, on a proposal from the rapporteur, has clarified the terms of these inclusions, defining all sites where preparation or processing of dangerous substances is planned, regardless of the type of processing, as covered by the seveso ii directive. we have also stated that this refers only to active plants or mines and not to simple deposits. secondly, the tragic accident at enschede has led the commission to redefine the provisions relating to explosives; the commission proposal was considered to be the most appropriate one to achieve the objective pursued, despite the various proposals put forward by the members. finally, the toulouse accident, which occurred in a climate of growing insecurity, still leaves an impressive mark on the collective memory. for technical and timing reasons, the question of ammonium nitrate, the substance responsible for the explosion, was not dealt with by the commission; the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. the question of ammonium nitrate is very complex and it has required many comparisons to establish, for the different types of ammonium nitrate, which division and which thresholds were appropriate to minimise the risks of accidents. the question is whether we should take the stricter position at european level in terms of thresholds or, on the basis of article 176 of the treaty, allow any state which deems it necessary to take further more restrictive measures, as it can already do. i personally propose to the house an amendment which provides for a higher threshold for the fourth category of products composed of ammonium nitrate, to ensure that farms are excluded from the scope of the directive without any possibility of error. there is one last opportunity, which i will mention very briefly and which we have taken up in our report: the commission has been asked to submit a proposal within a reasonable time to us to identify criteria and methodologies for spatial planning - another serious problem that has emerged - namely the location of these establishments. finally, as a final point, i would remind you that the commission has tried to strengthen the aspect of information to the public, which we consider to be particularly interesting and, above all, a duty towards our fellow citizens. i would like to conclude by thanking all the colleagues who have participated and collaborated and the committee secretariat.

mr president, at the recent world food summit in rome, 182 nations renewed their commitment to ending the tragedy of hunger in the world, where 800 million people are still undernourished. five years after the first summit in 1996, we regret to say that the target of halving their number by 2015 has largely failed. this gap between promises and reality must be bridged. the need to combat this tragedy is also reinforced by the fact that hunger is both a cause and an effect of poverty. a hungry man is not a free man; is a desperate man and can easily be persuaded to participate in desperate actions, such as conflict, international crime, drug trafficking, human trafficking, illegal immigration and terrorism. there is no doubt that more attention is needed from the western world, and the commitment to give back 0.7 percent of the gross domestic product of industrialized countries is more timely than ever, not least because, as john fitzgerald kennedy said, "no one can consider himself rich if his neighbors are poor". that is why we need concrete facts and plans. we must act now to prevent the two billion people who are now excluded from the welfare state, as shown by the demographic studies, from being added to the four billion people who are now excluded. the good governance of these developing countries remains, however, an essential condition for strengthening the cooperation which is indispensable to the achievement of the objectives set. access to information, as proposed by the italian prime minister berlusconi, and not disengagement, as mr rod has pointed out, and the new model of digitized state organization to combat corruption and increase efficiency would certainly make any use of development aid more transparent. the question of the proper functioning of the agency itself must also be urgently addressed through a conference of the states members of the fao. it is necessary to reform and streamline its operation and management in order to improve its transparency and efficiency and to achieve more appropriate actions and results. in johannesburg i will have the opportunity, together with the european parliament delegation, to see whether the european union is really capable of making and enforcing concrete political commitments with precise deadlines, the implementation of which must be based on effective partnership.
mr president, i think the commissioner and the president-in-office of the council are aware that this debate is suspected of being a serious case of hypocrisy. a few days ago, the director-general of the fao, jacques diouf, recalled that six years after the 1996 summit, 'the death knell is still ringing for the world's hungry'. all my colleagues have mentioned that 800 million people - 300 million of them children - are hungry and that 24 000 people die of hunger every day. mr diouf states: "promises have not been kept". worse, actions contradict words. what kind of action was expected? here are some examples: invest in the millennium goals, which is agriculture, health, education, bring the g8 countries' aid to this great battle to 0.7 percent of gross domestic product. we are a long way from that if we consider that the richest country, the united states, pays only 0.1 percent, or $34 per person. the damage is compounded by the mockery with which the rich countries have neglected this appointment. the president of the united states was absent, the president of russia was absent, the heads of government of japan, germany, great britain, france, canada were absent. only mr prodi, representing the european union, was present. all this casts a dangerous and malevolent shadow over the meeting on 26 august, the johannesburg summit. i think it would be appropriate to remind ourselves that we don't have much evidence yet to appeal to deal with and resolve this emergency.

the council. - mr president, first of all, i would like to congratulate the international community and all of us on the entry into force of the rome statute of the international criminal court on monday. this event must be considered one of the most decisive developments in international law since the second world war. the court's statute has been ratified by 69 countries and we can see that the statute already enjoys considerable support in the international community. the european parliament has repeatedly called for this. i myself called for this a few years ago in a report on human rights, which was adopted by a very large majority. it has been said and written by members of parliament. it is there now, and i think we should celebrate it here in parliament. the many international and internal conflicts which the world witnessed in the twentieth century underline the need for the swift establishment of this court. the criminal justice system can help make the world safer, more just and more peaceful. the very existence of the criminal court will be able to deter people from committing the grave crimes which, unfortunately, we have witnessed in our lifetime and until very recently - war crimes, genocide and other crimes against humanity. it is important that such crimes do not go unpunished, but that everyone be held accountable for their actions. the court of justice is therefore a key element in the strengthening of the international legal community. we must appeal to all states to join the rome statute. universal support is necessary for the court to function effectively. in order to achieve such universal support, we adopted a common position last year, which has recently been updated. on the basis of this common position, the european union has sought, through political dialogue and demarches, to achieve the widest possible support for the court from countries all over the world. the criminal justice system is a recurring theme in our relations with the united states, and it is precisely our discussions with the united states that are the subject of our debate today. the eu and the united states share the same fundamental values: freedom, democracy, human rights and the rule of law. that is why we have always considered it quite natural and necessary that the united states should be among the parties to the statute of the international criminal court. we have no doubt that the united states could make a very positive contribution to the court. at the 1998 diplomatic conference in rome we were fully aware of the concerns of the united states with regard to certain provisions of the statute. and we did our best to find ways and solutions to meet them - but unfortunately in vain. we regret to note that on 6 may this year the united states informed the secretary-general of the united nations that it did not intend to become a party to the statute, which had in fact been signed under the previous american administration. we believe that the united states has made a wrong decision. the european union has deeply regretted it. more recently, on 17 june, the general affairs council adopted conclusions expressing our concern at the present us draft law entitled 'american servicemembers' protection act', the so-called aspa. the latest version sets out restrictions on us participation in un peacekeeping operations, prohibits the transfer of information to the icc and prohibits us military assistance to the majority of participants in the court. as we said in our conclusions from the general affairs council in luxembourg, we believe that aspa could seriously undermine the work of the criminal court. we also underlined our concern about the provision which authorises the us president to use any means to release persons detained at the request of the court, including persons detained in eu member states. this provision has caused particular concern in the netherlands, which is to be the seat of the court. it has even been called aspa for the hague invasion act. if aspa is adopted, it will be a very unfortunate development for the international community. we have expressed our concern at all levels to the us government. our heads of delegation in washington have been dealing with this problem for a long time. it is a serious matter, a serious problem, a serious problem in the european-american relationship. but i would like to say that, although this is a major problem and a difficult situation, in my view we are not getting anywhere by describing the american bill as a threat to transatlantic relations. it would be unreasonable to bring it up in that atmosphere, and i would like to explain that. firstly, the icc is a global issue and not a bilateral problem between the us and the eu. it is essential for us not to be confrontational. we're not gonna get anything out of this. unfortunately, other major partners of the eu, such as china and india, are also opposed to the court. an associated country like turkey has not yet signed the statute or, moreover, has not subscribed to our common position or to any of the eu declarations in support of the court. as regards japan and russia, there is political will to accede to the statute, but it still lacks the necessary decision-making. nevertheless, our bilateral relations with all these countries have not been damaged or cooled by the fact that they are not yet parties to the court. we have been very careful to avoid confrontation on this issue, but at the same time we have tried to keep the court high on the agenda of our regular dialogue meetings. we have already convinced a number of countries through persistent lobbying in support of the statute, and we hope that in this way we can convince even more. i would also point out that the criminal court is not the only area where the united states and the european union disagree. friends have the right to disagree, but we will always - and i think this is wise - insist that what unites the eu and the us is, after all, stronger than what divides. we can all point to examples: steel (where we hope to find a solution soon), bananas (which were solved and there is much to be said about that), the kyoto protocol (where we continue our high-level dialogue). sometimes we find a solution, sometimes the disagreement continues. in the field of human rights, our views on the death penalty differ. but through our long-term efforts to combat the death penalty, we have succeeded in influencing american opinion. as an example, i would mention the recent us supreme court decision in the atkins case, which ruled out the death penalty for mentally handicapped persons. the eu has contributed to this case with an amicus curiae brief, which the us supreme court took into account. we will continue to pursue this policy. the us government has assured us that american intervention on the territory of an eu country would be - and i quote - "inconceivable". that has been said by both secretary of state powell and deputy secretary of state grossman. many american soldiers gave their lives for freedom and democracy in europe. i cannot imagine their grandchildren invade one of our member states. but the aspa proposal is now on the table, and section 3008 on the "use of force" will set a dangerous precedent in international law. i can assure you that we will be following this matter very closely. the court will soon be able to prove its worth as an independent and effective international judicial body. we in the european union will spare no effort to ensure its success. i am sure that those who are opposed to the criminal court today will be able to see for themselves that the rome statute both ensures the highest standards of legal certainty and protects against the use of the court for political purposes. we must face the fact that universal adherence to the court is a long way off. but i have confidence that at some point we will come through with our arguments, as we have done in the many other areas i mentioned earlier. the united states took a very far-reaching and regrettable step in its opposition to the court of justice on monday by vetoing it in the un security council. but i understand that negotiations on a compromise solution in the un security council will resume later today. it is essential that a solution is found which does not undermine the eu's common position and the statute of the court of justice, while maintaining the us involvement in peacekeeping operations. the presidency will do everything in its power to ensure that this happens.
commission. – mr president, two days ago the international criminal court entered into force. this is very much welcomed. bringing to justice those individuals who commit the most serious crimes against humanity, including genocide, widespread murder of civilians, torture and mass rape, is one of the major objectives of the eu's human rights policy. the creation of an international criminal court is central to this fight. by investigating and bringing to justice such individuals, the court provides an essential means of promoting respect for international humanitarian law and human rights. the european union stands firm in its commitment to the icc. now that the rome statute has entered into force, the icc is finally a reality. however, the hardest work still lies ahead of us. we need to give the icc real teeth so that it stands as a genuine disincentive to those who imagine they can get away with committing the most heinous crimes against humanity. in this context, the withdrawal by the united states of its signature from the rome statute came as a blow to the international community as it strives to prevent a repeat of the atrocities which have plagued recent conflicts. the fact that the world's greatest military power is not with us is a blow – there is no denying this. this is not the first time in recent history that europe has taken the lead and set the international agenda. many wrote off the kyoto protocol after the withdrawal of the united states, but the eu pressed on and ratified kyoto, setting an example which was followed by the global community to deliver a genuine prospect for tackling the problem of climate change. we intend to do the same to make the icc a working institution for global justice. as an independent nation, the united states has a sovereign right not to participate in the icc if that is its wish. in telling the world on 6 may that it did not intend to ratify the rome statute, the united states also gave assurances that it would not actively seek to undermine the work of the international criminal court, nor dissuade others from ratifying the rome statute. therefore the decision by the us senate on 6 june to adopt its own version of the american servicemembers' protection act (aspa), previously adopted by the us house of representatives, came as a great surprise and disappointment to many of america's allies and partners. we are hopeful that modifications can still be made to the text in the house and senate conference that would help dilute the impact of this legislation. the aspa's provisions, as currently drafted, are a grave cause for concern to supporters of the icc for several reasons. by attempting to prohibit military assistance to nations which ratify the icc, the aspa could dissuade countries from participating in it. by seeking to remove us personnel operating under un mandate from the jurisdiction of the icc, the aspa might restrict us participation in peace-keeping operations. we are already seeing the dramatic effect that this could have on the work of the un to maintain peace and stability in hot spots across the globe. the us move to oppose the renewal of the un's mission to bosnia-herzegovina threatens to undo years of work by the international community to rebuild that fractured community. the commission's first analysis identifies several potentially negative effects on the political environment and rule of law in bosnia-herzegovina. not least of these is the counter-terrorism work being carried out by the international police task force within bosnian territory. the eu is working around the clock with the un and other partners, including the united states, to find a solution to this crisis. but on one thing we stand firm. we will not allow the icc to be handicapped from birth by excluding the work of the united nations from its jurisdiction. there must be equality under the law regardless of nationality. there are further grounds for concern at the possible impact of the aspa. by prohibiting cooperation between its own judicial and law enforcement authorities and the icc, the aspa could set back the cause of the international fight against terror. last, but not least, there is a particularly disturbing provision authorising the president to use any means necessary to bring about the release of us personnel being detained at the request of the icc, including on the territory of eu member states. in the light of these considerations, the european union could not and did not remain silent. the eu reaction was discussed at the general affairs council of 17 june, where we adopted conclusions expressing our concerns at the aspa's provisions. we also agreed upon a strategy for presenting our concerns to the united states in a coordinated fashion. on 19 june the spanish ambassador to the united states, together with the commission's head of delegation in washington, presented an agreed statement on behalf of the eu member states to the us department of state. at the same time, eu ambassadors wrote to senior figures in the us administration, as well as to senior congressmen, conveying their grave concern at the contents of the aspa. on 20 june us ambassadors in eu capitals, as well as the us ambassador to the eu, were summoned to be informed of the eu's position. we sincerely hope that this series of interventions will persuade the us administration to withhold its support from this piece of legislation and prevent it from becoming us law. i trust that the council and the commission can rely on the full support of the european parliament in carrying through this strategy. i would therefore like to encourage you, as legislators, to take up this issue with your counterparts in the us carry this message to the us congress. i am looking forward to seeing parliament make its views known this afternoon in no uncertain way as you debate and adopt a resolution on this issue.

the commission (es) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, today we are dealing with a legislative package aimed at establishing the single european sky. the main objective of all these measures is simply to respond to the problem of congestion in european airspace without thereby reducing safety but, on the contrary, increasing it. once again, we must remember that this is our first concern and our priority, especially after the tragic accident in überlingen - where a number of fatalities were regretted - and where we had the feeling that it should have been and could have been avoided. what we want is to introduce a harmonised regulatory framework governing air traffic management in the european union, thus facilitating better airspace management and improved safety. i remember that the single sky was one of the initiatives announced by president prodi in the debate on his inauguration as a political priority for a europe close to the citizens. we have been working on this for three years, and today is the day to achieve concrete results. as regards the specific reports, i shall first refer to those by the rapporteurs, mr fava and mrs sanders-ten holte, which acknowledge the strategic importance and the maturity of the single sky initiative. i am pleased to note the support which the committee responsible has given to these proposals in parliament and i would once again like to thank the european parliament for its cooperation and work. as regards the amendments in particular, the commission is able to accept most of them; some with wording changes to better adapt them to the text, and others partially, since these amendments usually clarify or reinforce our initial proposals. however, the commission cannot accept and must therefore reject amendments nos 1, 2, 13, 19, 24, 27, 29, 34, 35 and 37 to 40 to mr fava's report and amendments nos 3, 12, 13, 14, 26, 46, 50, 51, 56, 57, 58, 59, 60, 61, 63, 66, 75, 77 to 80 and 83 to 107 to mrs sanders-ten holte's report. if i may, i would like to make a few comments on the amendments which are of greater relevance. first of all, i am thinking in particular of the ones concerning relations with eurocontrol. i agree that there is a need to establish proper cooperation between the community and this organization and, in fact, the technical negotiations for the community's accession to eurocontrol have already been concluded. as the honourable members are well aware, the formal agreement on the protocol for the community's accession to eurocontrol is due to be signed within a month, simply because of a problem of parliamentary agreement in one of the countries of the union. it is therefore not necessary to specify in the rules the arrangements for technical assistance to this organization, because we are going to be part of it. i believe that the amendments proposed in this connection either concern matters which are already adequately covered by the community's own accession to eurocontrol, or else they should be modified to adapt them to the nature of community acts. the same applies to the amendments calling for mandatory consultations. the commission does not question the principle of consultation with the social partners, but it would like this principle to be applied while respecting their right of initiative. as regards the nature of air traffic services, the legislative package has been carefully drafted to reconcile the requirements of the public interest with the need to support the dynamics of the sector. while recognising the inherent characteristics of these services, we cannot deny their economic impact in terms of the direct and indirect costs involved. the commission cannot therefore accept and rejects amendments nos 12 and 13 to mr fava's report. the same applies to a number of amendments which i have mentioned above and which we consider to be legally or technically incomplete and which we cannot support, as well as those which call for our proposal to be rejected as a whole. i would also like to add the following comments on certain amendments to mrs sanders-ten holte's report. amendment no 13, on the principle of separation between national surveillance authorities and air navigation service providers, affects the reasonable compromise reached during the negotiations in the high level group, where, i remind honourable members, all the countries of the union were represented, as well as norway and switzerland. i share the view that cooperation between the civil and military sectors is a key factor in the success of the single european sky and indeed our legislative proposals are already seeking to create the necessary conditions to stimulate such cooperation. but amendments nos 57 and 59 go beyond what the present division of powers and therefore the first pillar allows us to do. amendments nos 14 and 51 introduce redress mechanisms which are already provided for in national procedures. as regards the report by mrs maes on the safety of third country aircraft, this proposal aims to improve aviation safety by creating a system of inspection of third country aircraft to verify their compliance with international safety standards. the commission had already put forward a proposal on this subject in 1997, which had not been adopted until today because of the dispute over gibraltar airport. the proposal now before the house incorporates the provisions of the common position adopted by the council at the time, as well as the amendments adopted by the european parliament at second reading. the rapporteur, mrs maes, to whom i would like to thank, has signed up to this new proposal and the commission welcomes the report adopted by the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism. we are in a position to accept most of the 23 amendments, five of them with a different wording in terms of their principles and others with some changes in wording. however, seven amendments are problematic to the commission and i would therefore like to make the following observations: firstly, the list of shortcomings in amendment no 3 is restrictive in relation to the data available to the commission; secondly, amendment no 6 cannot be accepted either, since the proposal for a directive concerns only aircraft from third countries and not aircraft from the member states of the union; thirdly, the same can be said of amendment no 8, which would give the european aviation safety agency new responsibilities and this would require amendment of its constituent regulation, and amendment no 10, which falls outside the scope of the proposal for a directive. amendment no 14 does not seem to us to be necessary, since the commission proposal specifies that all complaints are admissible, and amendment no 15 would add a considerable amount of work to the aircraft inspection services, and yet the practical usefulness of the additional information requested seems to us to be more than doubtful. finally, amendment no 17 falls outside the scope of the inspections covered by the directive and would be contrary to the principles of the chicago convention and should therefore be integrated space governed by the same principles and the same rules. we are also well aware of the priorities, the main objectives of this important regulation: firstly, better use of airspace, which means reducing costs, better management to reduce delays, an increase in system capacity, but above all a significant strengthening of safety conditions, which remains our top priority. we also know called for. we believe that this is a fundamental step towards ensuring that the single sky is not just a list of good intentions but is really a regulatory certainty for all the countries of the european union. one last important point: the gradual opening up of the market, and hence of the market to competition, will take place within precise limits. we must remember that air traffic control mr president, the motion for a resolution tabled by the uen and those tabled by the other political groups are essentially aimed at establishing a credit line in the union budget to cover, in part, the damage caused by recent natural disasters in various member states or in the candidate countries. the need for a contingent community intervention was, moreover, an even trivial matter of course, considering the exceptional scale of the atmospheric phenomena which have struck europe as a whole. president prodi himself, visiting some of the disaster areas, together with the union's solidarity, could not but declare the union's ready readiness to intervene both with derogations and with financial contributions. the appropriateness of establishing a stable credit line is, in our view, based on further considerations. although many do not want to admit it, it is becoming evident that the climate in this world of ours is sadly changing, and this without resorting to catastrophism. of course, weather statisticians, going back over the years, are constantly trying to provide us with encouraging comparisons to help us reconsider the scale of disastrous events. however, it is not so much their size - however high - that is causing concern, but their close frequency and their repeated occurrence outside the traditional seasons for us europeans. the establishment of a stable credit line in the union budget therefore helps the states to deal with the damage caused by such events. the other part, the most significant part of the community's policy, is undoubtedly prevention. it is certainly useful to reconsider, both at national and community level, agricultural production policies, forestry policies and the management of areas at risk from hydrogeological damage; mr president, i should like to thank the rapporteur, mr beysen, for his thorough work and attention to all the problems which, as mr lehne, who preceded me, also mentioned, have been the subject of much discussion in the commission. i believe that the proposal in the form of a regulation is a workable proposal because i think that a regulation is really the most appropriate instrument for establishing uniform rules on specific and targeted issues, for ensuring price transparency, for strengthening legal certainty, for responding to the need for uniform rules with the introduction of the euro. moreover, the regulatory approach allows for the creation of a legal framework under which the consumer and other market players obtain sufficient information to make informed decisions. the text before us and voted on tomorrow is, however, the result of a thorough work in committee and in the committees responsible for opinion, which amends and improves the original proposal on many important aspects relating to protection, guarantees for consumers, for minors, for small and mediumsized enterprises, for healthy competition and the introduction of the subsidiarity mechanism. the amendment introduces the principle of subsidiarity, under which member states may partially restrict commercial communications for reasons relating to consumer protection, competition and the protection of suppliers. i think that what was voted on in the legal affairs committee is particularly significant, namely the strengthening of the protection of minors, particularly with regard to personal data, gifts and prizes which are potentially harmful. the consumer is also protected against judicial and extrajudicial proceedings. overall, i think it is a balanced proposal, which takes account of the need to make the internal market operational and, at the same time, takes account of the need to protect consumers.
mr president, commissioner, rapporteur, i think that the proposal for a regulation now before parliament should be welcomed because, while it is true that promotional sales are a phenomenon and represent a market share which is far from negligible, it is also true that certain national laws are still in force today, with the restrictions they impose on promotions, particularly on sales below cost, which in fact undermine the establishment of the internal market. i believe that the commission has proposed a balanced text which adequately addresses the problem of the absence of a genuine internal market for promotions and sales, fragmented by different laws prohibiting in some countries certain behaviour which is permitted in others. i fear that some of the amendments proposed by the committee on legal affairs and citizens' rights risk undermining the effectiveness of this text. i refer in particular to amendments nos 29 and 32, which, although they are defending the principle of subsidiarity, are in fact likely to undermine what the regulation says and proposes on the subject of under-cost sales. i think we should say something first. there are competition authorities at community level and at national level. i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. there are competition authorities, but in all other cases, under-cost sales are not only not bad but are a good thing. i am not saying that the commission should not be involved in this, but i am saying that it should be involved in the negotiations. and it is not true, in my view, that under-costing is necessarily a disadvantage for small businesses; in fact, small firms often resort to under-selling to launch a product, to launch a business, as they do not have large financial resources for large-scale promotional campaigns or, often, not even on a small scale. i think that would be a risky harm to consumers and businesses. another one. the question of inflation. i am thinking of italy, but not only: the commission has also taken the view that the introduction of a system of penalties for under-pricing, as in italy, has made it virtually impossible to sell at below cost, and this has contributed to creating the conditions for a less competitive market and thus a market more exposed to price inflation.
mr president, commissioner, if the objective is regulation which offers full legal certainty and at the same time a rule by which citizens derive the maximum benefit from the internal market, then the regulation which has been presented to us has certainly taken the optimum direction. we have worked a lot on this regulation; the number of amendments mentioned by my colleagues and the debate in the legal affairs committee have shown the importance of what we consider to be a necessary path for the europe we want to build. the internal market needs rules and the rules need to be tested in everyday life. the regulation opens up a number of extremely important areas. i am not quoting those who have already mentioned my colleagues. on one point, for example, we would like to see more reflection: the one on the settlement of disputes. we would also like to try out some self-regulation experiments in this new world of consumers confronting the market. we also call on the commission to develop this pilot phase of the european extrajudicial network, in connection with the contentious element which is present in every commercial moment. we also want to see the work of the expert group on commercial communications increased, as my colleagues have suggested. this group, set up in 1998, now has to adapt to the ever more pressing construction of the internal market. there are also a number of points, which i have already mentioned, on which we are in full agreement. in conclusion, we believe that this is the right way to promote the idea of the europe we want in the internal market.

in writing. - (it) congratulations to the rapporteur on the work he has done. state aid must take shape and become concrete at exceptional moments in the economic life of a nation. if aid became a recurrent and well-established fact, rather than creating benefits in the territory and providing the necessary conditions for overcoming difficult times, it would certainly aggravate the problems of those who benefited. this is the view that should be taken of the berenguer fuster report on the draft commission regulation on the application of articles 87 and 88 of the ec treaty to state aid for employment, which considers that these articles should normally apply to the transport sector as well. the forthcoming enlargement must be regarded as an exceptional event of extraordinary importance. it will reveal a different distribution of labour, as well as profound differences in wages and living standards, between the present member states and the new members. possible structural distortions, caused by the certainly lower labour costs in these countries, by different environmental, social and technical criteria and by a clear competition between labour forces in the market, can be addressed with more flexibility in the labour market and, in part, with state employment aid. the enlargement to new member states will lead to surpluses of labour, especially in the traditional economic sectors of heavy industry, agriculture and transport; the first is that the unemployed will not be able to find work immediately in the new emerging economic sectors. in writing. - (it) we voted in favour of the report by mr berenguer fuster. it would have been difficult not to do so, given the purpose of the aid and the commission's objectives of simplification and transparency. however, it is worth reflecting on the problem posed by the fact that the commission is not unaware that in certain regions of the member states of the union the difference between being or not being in the area of aid provided for in article 87 (3) (c) represents for undertakings more than 12 per cent less in terms of taxation. the question then arises is the content of article 4 (3) of the proposed regulation, which refers specifically to the abovementioned regions. the commission is aware that the method used to define these areas does not allow us to define precisely which areas are actually disadvantaged. the method used by local work systems to draw up these maps and, in some cases, the deviations from this method are worth considering. we therefore believe that it is appropriate to review the current maps to check their consistency, irrespective of the fact that the regions themselves use them, because otherwise the proposed regulation, even with the 10% increase on the maximum, would actually have the objective, in such cases, of covertly and only partially correcting the errors made.
