mr president, the wars, the soviet presence and the taliban have left a state without institutions, without industry and with a landless agriculture, with levels of poverty and illiteracy, even of return, not only female, truly unimaginable. moreover, the lack of integration between the different cultural, social, religious and ethnic identities that make up afghan society further accentuates the complexity of the problem that the transitional government faces every day. to govern this country, as has been said, means not only making the necessary institutional reforms, starting with the constitution, but also quickly creating, starting from scratch, a basic credit system, spreading education, respect among citizens and ethnic groups, rebuilding cities and infrastructure, separating military life from civilian life, reinventing an industry and agriculture capable of surviving in a globalized world. for the transitional government, the challenge is not trivial, because it is a question of acting on everything simultaneously in the fastest, most cost-effective and participatory way possible. it is not easy to do this, especially if it has to be done in a relatively short period of time. karzai has made an explicit commitment to achieve a stable peace between citizens, between ethnic groups and between the sexes, in order to create the basis for the democratization of the country during the two years of transitional government. however, as commissioner patten said, the road is still very winding. the situation of women in particular, despite karzai's statements, has not actually improved. female literacy is at unimaginable levels: 6 to 7 per cent is the data against 39 per cent of the previous situation. the new government, from this point of view, has also deteriorated: some warlords have taken on political roles, not only in the decentralized administrations but also in the government in kabul. censorship has increased, as has been mentioned; the committee on petitions has already adopted a number of amendments. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i think that it is never superfluous to talk about european citizenship and that it is never too much to talk about, also because citizens are often expected to be european without being recognised as such. in fact, citizens begin to feel european, and they begin to feel european the moment they begin to converse with the european institutions. citizenship is something more, it seals a bit of membership of this european dimension in which the citizen must feel constructive and responsible at a time of great momentum and dynamism. we think that the turnout in the european elections is low and is falling more and more, but let us ask ourselves: what assurance do we give to the citizens of our member states that they are europeans? we do not guarantee a right to education in reciprocity between member states; we don't have a problem with listening to languages. we do not insure a right to work; we are not ensuring, as the rapporteur, mr coelho, who has made an excellent report, has said, free movement. we do not recognise qualifications, therefore we do not recognise a right to work. we do not recognize the right to health. i say this as a citizen because i receive petitions from citizens to the committee on petitions of the european parliament, where they describe these great intolerance within the member states of the union. i would like to point out a great contradiction: we have made schengen, which is a milestone to offer the whole world and especially to the countries where there are still territorial and border wars, but we maintain the right of the member states to expel citizens of the european union from one member state to another. is it possible that there is still a right of expulsion or is it contrary to schengen? we can expel citizens outside the schengen borders, not within the same territory. i think we should therefore make every effort to build this europe from the citizens, starting with this recognition of status which the bill of rights rightly placed at the centre of its efforts and which must be recovered within the treaties. if we cannot determine this, we may make many conventions but we will not succeed in building europe, especially when one country - i am referring to ireland, but there could be many others, including my own - refused to recognise, sign and vote in favour of the nice document and when three member states have not agreed to share our experience of the single currency. and then the road is long: let us all strive to build this europe around the citizens!
mr president, commissioner, despite the great strides made in recent years towards genuine european citizenship, much remains to be done to guarantee fundamental rights equally for all. that is what which aims to guarantee all citizens equal opportunities, free movement, residence throughout the community, free access to work, justice and all rights, with innovative openings also for third country nationals. these basic principles are accompanied by a commitment to guaranteeing everyone a real job, a real home, adequate healthcare and prospects for growth, both social and economic. in mr president, commissioner, i am returning to the second reading of this report, which has already seen a frank, sometimes even lively, confrontation in this house between those who want the citizens to be fully involved in the decision-making process on certain structural policies and those who instead want greater powers and autonomy for the political, technical and administrative institutions responsible for this task. in its assessment of the first reading, the council has in a sense downsized the rapporteur's proposals, considering them perhaps too advanced, too open to democratic participation which could slow down the legislative process, or which could allow, as the rapporteur herself said a short while ago, excessive, authoritarian or distorting interpretations. in summary, the council intends to give a consultative role - yes, important but not decisive - to citizens' organisations, placing the task of deciding on the basis of the input from civil society fully in the hands of elected legislators, but without imposing any mandatory requirements. the rapporteur proposes various forms of judicial redress in cases where there is a conflict between the views of citizens and the decisions of the competent authority, especially when the matter involves important issues such as safety, the environment and public health. as regards the need to guarantee member states the possibility of derogating from this directive in an emergency, there is a specific amendment which provides for this loophole in full respect of subsidiarity and of particular environmental conditions or quotas. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environmentally friendly aspects of the environment. many of the amendments were accepted by the council, and some of them restate principles of particular importance, i would even say fundamental. let us consider a few examples: the first of these is that the public must be able to obtain useful information by using electronic means, which allow access to the documents of the institutions. secondly, the public must receive, inter alia, information concerning the right to participate in decision-making in the forms and measures permitted, which we have briefly mentioned above. thirdly, the public must have the right to make comments, including on the merits, and to take positions without prejudice to the public. there is still an obligation on the competent authorities to make reasonable efforts, so to speak, to be able to respond to the public both individually and collectively. the commission has also proposed that the member states should adopt practical, concrete provisions on appeal procedures and provide the public with all the necessary information on the administrative and judicial means of access to such appeals. this is to ensure that citizens have the opportunity to defend their own disagreement, which is different from that of the established authority, up to the last possible stage of the trial. this concept will, of course, be interpreted differently in different countries, depending on the degree of democracy in the various countries which allows public participation and defends, above all, the organizations through which the public exercises this right of participation. this twofold moment seems particularly important: first, access to the competition and to the drafting of legislative acts; second, in the event of disagreement, the possibility of appealing to the final instance. this is to go back to the basic philosophy of voltaire who said, "dear friends, i don't share any of your ideas, but i would give my life so that you can defend them to the end". europe, if it doesn't teach us law, at least teaches us a little philosophy.

states on the treatment and disposal of waste – a controversial issue in a number of member states but, nonetheless, one that has to be addressed with courage and effectiveness. mr mulder referred to the food and veterinary office. it is doing a very good job in ensuring compliance with community law. its reports continue to highlight the serious shortcomings in the implementation of legislation. coming forward with a new proposal to improve controls. as i have said repeatedly, we must make it painful and costly not to respect community law. mr mulder mentioned a quality mark. this may be valuable but it has its limitations. like legislation, quality marks are only effective if the qualifying conditions are respected. in the netherlands, for instance, feed producers undertook to use only safe ingredients as part of their quality assurance scheme. clearly, they failed to respect this requirement. so quality marks may be useful but they have their limitations. mr whitehead referred to the rapid alert system at community level and this has worked very effectively in relation to the recent food-safety crises. in a number of cases – not just this one but also the nitrofen case – madam president, the excellent report by mrs gutiérrez is a highly significant event, first of all because it is the first of its kind and organic to be presented to this parliament. in recent years and especially since lisbon, there has been talk of the need to develop a 'europe of knowledge', but so far this has remained in many respects an unrealized intention. those who have experienced the effects of the erasmus and socrates programmes in universities, as i have, even if they are often limited in scope because of insufficient funds, know how important they are both for broadening the perspective of students and teachers and for forming a european sensibility in the wider context of citizens, starting with the families of those who have benefited from them. the aim is now to extend the union's attention and involvement to many other aspects of university life, first of all by encouraging the dissemination of good practice from some countries to all the other countries of the union, by promoting the right to study of all citizens, regardless of their economic conditions, which is achieved by strengthening public university education, the only source of investment not dominated by the logic of immediate profit and therefore able to guarantee all citizens the possibility of accessing higher education, necessary to renew the ruling classes. we do not hide the fact that the primacy of public universities in some countries of the union is today threatened by dangerous tendencies towards privatization, which are fatally likely to undermine the freedom of studies and to reduce the level of research and preparation of students by favouring the census over merits and abilities. the gutiérrez report takes account of this situation and makes a number of significant proposals. i would also like to stress that it asks the commission to set up a european university house where the academic world - from students to teachers, from the various agencies involved in the field - can express their needs and formulate their proposals. this would be an interesting application of the concept of subsidiarity to a sector of european culture which is central to all our work.

the rapporteur. mr president, the report i am about to present concerns the commission's green paper on compensation for victims of crime. it is certainly a very complex problem from a legal point of view, but fortunately an important debate is taking place on this subject, with the aim of identifying the appropriate legislative instruments and also the financial resources to guarantee what should be the fundamental right of the victim of a crime: to obtain legitimate compensation for suffering and damage suffered, in particular when the offender is absent, in the sense that he is not identifiable or is not able to compensate the victim. we know, moreover, that the number of victims of crime in crossborder situations is increasing dramatically, due primarily to the increased movement of citizens within the union but also, unfortunately, to the increase in crime in general and in particular in very serious and important crime, such as terrorism, paedophilia and trafficking in human beings. it is also worth noting that victims often suffer in two ways: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the protection of the rights of the child is guaranteed. for all these reasons, when the main guidelines for the creation of a genuine area of freedom, security and justice were set out, tampere already explicitly indicated the need to establish minimum standards for the protection of victims of crime, especially as regards their access to justice and their right to compensation. unfortunately, since 1999, this strong political determination has not yet produced any significant legislative outcome at community level. the primary objective is therefore to create, as soon as possible, common minimum standards to give effect to the right to compensation throughout the european union, both for european citizens and for those who reside legally in europe. such legislation must contain a clear, precise and agreed definition by all member states of the types of crime and injury which may give rise to compensation. it will also be necessary to identify, with the same precision and sharing, the persons who may legally be the recipients of compensation, considering, inter alia, that sometimes the families and dependants of those who have suffered a crime are indirect victims of crime. the identification of these minimum standards is certainly not an easy process, for two reasons: the first concerns the objective difficulty of legal codification, since a complex process of approximation of national legislation, which is currently very different, must be initiated. the second plea in law concerns the essential need to obtain adequate resources. there are various ways of obtaining funds for this purpose. the commission suggests that a special solidarity fund could be set up at community level, to which the proceeds from the confiscation and subsequent sale of assets belonging to criminal networks could also be allocated. the identification of rules and procedures as harmonised as possible with regard to the treatment of the victim remains a priority objective. this would help to resolve the sometimes abnormal differences between the different systems of the member states. at present there are differences, and therefore discrimination, which are unacceptable to the detriment of the victims, with regard to the place of residence of the victim or with regard to the state in which the crime was committed. in fact, a situation of objective disparity of treatment linked to the country in which the offence occurs is created, thus resulting in a clear violation of the fundamental principle of non-discrimination.
the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, this proposal for a directive, for which i am the rapporteur, aims to establish common minimum standards to ensure adequate intervention in favour of genuine economic assistance for citizens who are unable to bear the costs of a legal proceeding in which they are involved. it is an initiative that fits perfectly into the project of creating an area of freedom, security and justice in the territory of the union in which all citizens are guaranteed to have their fundamental rights respected, regardless of their economic situation. the original legal basis is article 61 of title iv of the european treaty which says that, in order to achieve this objective, the council must provide for measures in the field of judicial cooperation in civil matters. the tampere european council responded to this call by establishing minimum standards for legal aid in crossborder cases: let's highlight this passage. the commission took a more bold step by proposing to extend aid to domestic cases. the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs has accepted the challenge and adopted the commission's opinion on the scope of the directive: i am not saying that we should not be concerned with the problems of the community. the legal basis must therefore be extended and must now be sought not only in article 61 but also in article 65 of the treaty. furthermore, the charter of fundamental rights of the european union also helps us in this opening up of the field of application, namely article 47 (3) which says that legal aid is foreseeable for those who do not have sufficient resources to obtain equal opportunities in access to justice. it is the first time that we have taken up this type of aid at community level with conviction. there is therefore also a good opportunity to invite those member states - and there are many - which already provide for specific judicial assistance for their own citizens to join in the process of harmonization. the report, which was unanimously approved by the committee responsible in this parliament, goes even further. it proposes to extend the assistance from the actual judicial phase to the pre-litigation phase, in the knowledge that effective mediation, an attempt to bring the parties to a settlement, often avoids even the passage to the actual trial, thus limiting and excluding all inconvenience for the citizens concerned but, above all, limiting costs. this double opening could lead - it is true - to an increase in the costs borne by the member states. however, the political scope and social dimension of a directive conceived in this way would justify - and indeed does justify - parliament's call on the council to take this step. we have the primary task here of indicating the political objectives which will help to build a europe of citizens, a europe of equal justice for all. i would like to conclude this presentation by commenting on an unpredictable, even somewhat disconcerting, initiative of the council's last hour, which sent - it is true, only by way of information and informally - a new text with the clear intention of re-emphasizing article 1, which limits the scope of application to crossborder cases only. in short, the attempt is to - would be to - question everything, to point and re-point and start a debate again. apart from the substance of this matter, which goes against the unanimous vote of the parliamentary committee, there is also a serious defect in form and procedure. the committee on civil liberties has decided, by express vote, to complete the whole procedure until the report based on the text of the executive committee is adopted, or at any rate presented in this house, in accordance with the most elementary rules of the consultation procedure. if this parliament were to accept the council's stop or any proposal for referral back to committee, there would be very important consequences in interinstitutional legal relations, but also in the consultation procedure, with a serious breach of the rules laid down by the treaty. the prerogatives of the european parliament would thus be undermined and a very serious precedent would be set for the future. this report must therefore proceed - that is the wish of the committee - until the end of its normal course, that is, until it is put to the vote of this parliament. in conclusion, i would like to ask the commission, and commissioner vitorino in particular, for an opinion on this situation.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial interests are protected. mr president, the legal affairs committee, in its opinion on the green paper on compensation for victims of crime, welcomes the approach proposed and adopted by the commission and shares the identification of the three main objectives of possible action at community level: first, the opportunity to ensure that victims of crime within the union can obtain compensation from the state, i.e. to provide a safety net for all residents of the union; second, the need to take measures to limit the unfair effects which may result from the wide disparity between the levels of compensation provided for in the various member states, which in practice depend on the member state of residence of the victim or the member state in which the victim was the victim of the crime; third, the possibility of facilitating access to state compensation for victims in a crossborder situation, that is to say, of ensuring that victims' access to state compensation is not too dependent on the place within the union where the crime was committed. however, the committee on legal affairs and citizens' rights has made some comments - i thank the rapporteur, mr angelilli, for this - which essentially accepted all the amendments contained in the opinion of the committee on legal affairs and citizens' rights, according to which compensation should cover the material and non-material damage suffered by the victim. sufficiently long time limits are required for the state to submit a claim for compensation; the same applies to the dies a quo, i.e. the date from which the limitation period is calculated, in order to avoid any difference in treatment. it is also essential that uniform forms of claim for compensation be drawn up in all the community languages and that provision be made for minimum procedural guarantees such as, inter alia, the right to a fair trial, the right to be represented by a lawyer, the right to access to the procedure, and easier access for crossborder victims to compensation from the state. in conclusion, the community initiative on compensation for victims would indeed make an important contribution to the construction of a european area of freedom, security and justice.

absolute readiness he has shown to take up the suggestions which have emerged during the debate in committee. the balance of women's representation in decision-making bodies is a problem that has been raised many times and on which europe has often stressed the need to intervene, but which is by no means solved. as the commissioner has also pointed out, there is a democratic deficit in this respect, affecting all sectors of society: the economic, the social and the political. the report is intended to take stock of the social dimension, that is, the representation of women in the social partners. in tackling this, the first thing that comes to mind is the lack of systematic data. information on the presence of women in the organisational structures of decision-making bodies within the social partners is scarce; the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work is based on the principle of equal treatment for men and women. in fact, it must be admitted that the european trade union confederation has tried to gather information and data, but has encountered many difficulties because of the lack of cooperation of the national federations. what emerges, however, from the available studies is a pyramidal structure, with women representing some 40% of the total enrolment, a proportion that falls to less than half as one reaches the decision-making structures. even more scarce information is available on employers' organizations. this has resulted in a very low representation of women in the negotiating delegations, which also affects the results of equal opportunities policy. in fact, in recent years, at the instigation of europe, a number of strategies have been put into effect, varying according to the reality of the member states, which have led to an improvement in the situation, although it still remains completely unsatisfactory. in italy, for example, a policy of positive action within trade union organisations has been implemented, encouraged by legislation and the funding of specific training projects, to encourage the presence of women in the governing bodies, and which in many cases has resulted in the introduction of quotas in the statutes of the organisations. all this has led to significant positive results, but almost exclusively at the territorial level: the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. there is a direct link between the presence of women in decision-making bodies and negotiating delegations and the pursuit of a policy of equal opportunities. this link is also confirmed by the results of a research project promoted by the dublin foundation on the subject of 'equal opportunities and collective agreements in the union', which shows that the presence of female negotiators has produced results in terms of reducing existing inequality, more attention to reconciling work and family, and unequal pay between men and women. it is therefore necessary, as called for in mrs smet's report, for the european commission to start collecting data and to create a database on the presence of women in the social partners, in order to be able to define indicators to strengthen the presence in decision-making bodies, to create a database of the results of collective bargaining in the framework of equal opportunities, to be used later on for the dissemination of good practice, to encourage the social partners to create networks between female negotiators and female members of the management board so that they can exchange experience and knowledge and to further develop their assigned role in promoting equal opportunities in the framework of employment policy. the development of social dialogue at european level will certainly benefit in terms of weight, effectiveness and positive results in the pursuit of the objectives if a balance of gender representation is developed at all levels, including in the socioeconomic field.

mr president, i would not express a positive or negative opinion on the johannesburg earth summit: it is perhaps enough to say that this was a necessary and useful meeting, even if the optimism of rio 10 years ago has given way to a certain mistrust of the timing and the objectives to be achieved. the adoption of both an action plan - which includes reference to poverty reduction, health, technology transfer and trade - and a political declaration on a global commitment to work together for a better use and distribution of natural and energy resources is an ambitious goal for both developed and developing countries to achieve a rebalancing of the world's north-south relationship and the sustainability of development and progress policies. i hope, however, that this conference was not just a catwalk for heads of state or government, but rather that it highlighted how central the issues of sustainable development must be in the international political agenda today. the need for supranational governance, which is steadily investing in the planet's many environmental, economic and social problems, with particular attention to the poor and developing countries, was felt in johannesburg. the debt issue of poor and developing countries is also a central issue, which has a substantial impact on the success of the strategy for sustainable development in the medium and long term. in this connection, the question of transparency, through the computerization of the budgets of developing countries, is an essential condition for continuing on the road to the cancellation of past debts.

- madam commissioner, i believe that the continuous reference to the lisbon objectives is not very useful if action plans and regulatory measures are to be drawn up at european level and above all at the level of individual countries, with a view to creating the best environment for the competitiveness of enterprises, especially at this time, and thus creating the conditions for good employment. i think there are a number of things that can be done - that you can choose to do or not do - at the level of individual countries. some points to consider: i believe, for example, that the continuous call for the intervention of the social partners is not only excessive but risks leading us down a path of further tightening of the labour markets, a path which is to protect and give guarantees, insurance, opportunities to workers and companies already in the productive circle, thus defending the insiders of the labour market and the economy, thus creating more obstacles for the outsiders, those who need it most, those who are looking for a job. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i would remind you, however, that there are problems of mobility within the community, within individual countries: i am thinking, for example, of italy, where there is very little, almost no, labour mobility within the country, and this is because of labour market legislation, because of national collective agreements - i hope no one wants to propose a european contract for the various sectors of labour - agreements which do not recognise the specificities and even the comparative advantages that individual areas can provide for an efficient labour market; mr president, i should like to begin by saying how necessary it is to lay the foundations for a common policy among all the member states on immigration strategies, on the fight against illegal immigration and, therefore, on a common definition of the right of asylum. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work. it is essential to distinguish clearly between immigration, illegal immigration, trafficking in human beings and the right to asylum, a right which must retain its valuable specific character of protecting human rights. in this context, the report, following a supposedly open and progressive logic, extends the right of asylum, which is fundamental and therefore not extendable to excess, excessively and improperly: firstly, because it effectively equates those seeking protection with those seeking refugee status. secondly, because the report proposes a definition of the consequent right of asylum that is too broad for family members. in fact, family members who are eligible for international protection include same-sex partners and their children; in the same way, when it comes to minors, other family members can also be considered as de facto parents, and therefore it is not necessary to have lived together with the applicant in the country of origin. so if there are no major changes through the amendments, especially as regards the restriction of the definition of 'family' in the context of the right of reunification, my group will vote against.
mr president, despite the excellent work of mrs cederschiöld, who has considerably improved the commission's proposal, we shall vote against because there are at least four fundamental problems which cannot and must not be underestimated: first, the all-european obsession to over-regulate the internet through special laws; secondly, the creation of an area of justice, freedom and security based on the harmonization of the number of years of imprisonment that can be served; thirdly, the repressive approach, which requires the necessary criminalisation of all behaviour which can be considered as attacks on information systems; fourthly, the illusion that the repression of criminal phenomena can be achieved by tightening penalties, rather than by improving the effectiveness of controls. in essence, we believe that it would be preferable to tackle the issue of crimes committed online through the instruments of criminal law that already exist rather than multiplying specific legislation defined on a technological basis, which, moreover, has the shortcomings i have mentioned. it is on the basis of these considerations that we shall vote against. in substance, these problems were also raised by mr cederschiöld and mr coelho. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect.

ladies and gentlemen, we often hide behind - and i am speaking of course of the whole political class - the observance of rules and procedures, without ever really trying to change them or force them, in a positive sense, of course: that is the message i want to send on the sidelines of this debate. the 2003 budget is a good budget, and i congratulate the rapporteurs on their commitment, their hard work and the results achieved, also thanks to the commissioner, mrs schreyer, the whole commission structure, the secretariat and the rapporteurs, but i cannot help but stress that this is a technical budget in which our role has been primarily to settle accounts, without having the strength, courage or will to take real political action. we young people may sometimes wish to change the world, but this time i would be content to change just a few things in our european budget.
mr president, a 'thank you' goes to the rapporteurs, the chairman of the committee on budgets and the commissioner. we have already said that as a liberal group we are quite satisfied with this budget, which seems to us to be absolutely rigorous and transparent. this is part of our culture. i would add, however, that in my view it is also an overly technical budget and only timidly political. its basic outlines are acceptable, particularly as regards reform and enlargement, which i consider to be the most important challenge we face. but precisely because it is a challenge, we must make a political commitment, more decisively and, above all, more visibly for all european citizens. i too believe, as the chairman of the committee said a moment ago, that the procedure must be reformed. the technical development of the procedure, simplification and, in particular, cultural and political development are needed, with the council's powers being delimited in an optimal manner, not reductive, for a more fruitful, more attentive and above all more contingent dialogue. we need a basic philosophy of the european budget, a basic philosophy which means shared, not concentrated - the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, at a delicate moment in the civil aviation sector, whose future we have recently discussed in this house with the single european sky rules, the european commission has proposed a new regulation on compensation and assistance to passengers in the event of denied boarding. the liberalisation of air transport has brought many benefits to passengers; the competition on many air routes has brought down prices and diversified routes and destinations, but consumers have good reason to complain: denied boarding and cancelled flights create considerable disappointment, and assistance during excessive delays too often leaves much to be desired. many of us in this house have experienced such inconveniences because of the frequency of our flights, and it is therefore very easy in this case to put ourselves in the place of the citizens and to understand that effective protection of their rights must be guaranteed by new legislation. in view of the shortcomings of the existing legislation, the european commission proposes to tackle the issue differently: the commission has also proposed a number of measures to help the victims of the accident, including a call for volunteers, inspired by the effective us system, and a deterrent system, which obliges airlines to compensate passengers more for the damage suffered. in addition, protection is being substantially extended, as we shall see shortly. but we must not ignore the global context in which this proposal is being put forward. we have had a very constructive debate in the committee on transport, which has looked at all the aspects of the matter. as the commissioner has just mentioned, overbooking, the main cause of denied boarding, is a marginal phenomenon compared to the annual flow of air passengers in the community. in order to protect a minimum group of passengers, the risk of penalizing the entire spectrum of travellers with a possible generalised price increase cannot be taken. we must be very careful and define precisely, also in the light of the economic impact, the best solutions to achieve the objective without generating negative consequences. in this context, madam commissioner, i regret that the commission has provided little statistical support for its proposal. we need concrete data, facts, to decide, and this lack of data has certainly created a number of difficulties in the drafting of my report. i now summarize the main topics on which we worked to produce the final document. the first is the definition: i think that it is essential from a methodological point of view to define more precisely all the actors involved and the terms used, in order to avoid any confusion to the detriment of both passengers and airlines. the commission has also adopted a number of amendments to specify the details of article 2. the second point concerns tour operators: passengers who have purchased an 'all inclusive' ticket are already more than adequately protected by directive 90/314. the commission proposal therefore risks creating confusion as regards the reference text, to the detriment, in particular, of passengers. it was therefore necessary - as we have done - to limit the liability of tour operators under this regulation to passengers only, seats only. finally, the most controversial point is compensation for passengers in the event of denied boarding: the commission proposal has given rise to a great deal of discussion and a great deal of confusion. neither the criteria for the new compensation nor the impact assessment convinced the members of the committee on transport. what is important to us is to maintain a balance between the protection of passengers and the vitality of an important economic sector such as air transport. we therefore proposed a division into three distance bands and a reduction in the amount of compensation. we must remember that it is not the compensation but the implementation of the voluntary system that we must aim at. i also think it is quite inappropriate to extend compensation to excessive delays for several reasons: firstly, because in writing. -(it) the fundamental right to privacy and, in particular, the right to the confidentiality of communications, are today in danger: in the fight against terrorism, states have limited - or are progressively preparing to limit - the guarantees that protect citizens and are provided for by law, in particular by article 8 of the european convention on human rights and by the case law resulting from it, by article 7 of the eu charter of fundamental rights, by directives 95/46/ec, 97/66/ec and 2002/58/ec. the belief that terrorism can be fought by limiting the freedoms and rights of citizens is a delusion, as the echelon example shows. even the systematic and widespread interception of the content of communications implemented by echelon - a system now perfected by the rules in preparation on the collection of data on insider trading - was not able to prevent the terrorist attacks of 11 september or the other dramatic events that followed, because, in reality, this system is entirely focused on industrial espionage. the only effect of echelon - whose illegality is obvious and unquestionable - is to ignore the law and the rule of law, to impede free competition in the market and to endanger democracy, citizens' rights and freedoms.
in writing. -the echelon system and the interception of citizens' communications are still the subject of a completely incomprehensible hypocrisy: the hypocrisy of the member states which, although part of the echelon system, do not know of its existence; hypocrisy of those member states - and in particular the netherlands, france and germany - which, although not participating in the echelon system, have developed and activated systems performing exactly the same functions of intercepting citizens' international and national communications through keywords; the commission's proposal to amend the directive on the protection of the euro against counterfeiting is based on the hypocrisy of the european parliament, which decided not to grant itself the powers of inquiry which would have allowed it to carry out a series of checks on the existence and operation of echelon. although echelon is a totally illegal system under international, european and national law, no european institution and no member state is intervening to protect citizens' rights by bringing an action for invasion of privacy. if the objective - as regards echelon or interceptions - is to achieve a european intelligence system, let us ask that this system be subject to the basic rules of democracy or that the law be truly transparent, that it be clearly regulated, that it be subject to democratic and judicial control and that guarantees be provided for citizens.

the rapporteur. madam president, commissioner, in my view, and perhaps also in the view of the majority of the committee, the two joint reports this evening have been presented in a very hasty manner and, from a technical point of view, they are certainly not up to the legal tradition of europe or its member states. the central point of these two reports is in particular the approximation of legislation on the confiscation of property, instruments and proceeds of crime. specifically, it concerns the possibility of extended confiscation, that is to say, confiscation not only of property arising from a criminal offence but also of all other property which, although not arising from a criminal offence, belongs to a person who has been sentenced to a very serious prison sentence and who is unable to prove that the property has a lawful origin. this part of the report, commissioner vitorino, has been deleted by the committee, so what remains is a possibility of confiscation of the proceeds of crime. but a framework decision is not necessary to achieve this result in the european community, because almost all european countries have the mandatory consequence in their legislation of confiscation of property derived from crime, or at least the possibility of it. it was precisely to overcome the difficulty the committee had in accepting the reversal of the burden of proof, with an amendment which closely resembled italian legislation - amendment no 11 to article 3 (1) - that i had suggested the possibility of confiscating surplus assets - that is, assets subject to extended confiscation - only when the prosecution had proved that they were disproportionate to the activity carried out by the person or that they were not assets corresponding to those declared for tax purposes by the person himself. the person was then given the opportunity to prove the legitimate origin of these goods: there was therefore a mitigation, but not a reversal, of the burden of proof. this has puzzled, impressed and perplexed the committee, which has therefore rejected my amendment as well. i therefore propose that members approve this amendment because only then can we introduce into legislation the extension of confiscation, which is one of the objectives of the proposal and which, in my view, is also a useful tool in the fight against organised crime. it is based on two principles: the prosecution must prove the disproportion of the subject's assets, that is, it must prove that these assets are greater than its real assets or are greater than the income declared for tax purposes, while the subject has the right to prove that these assets have a legal origin. if, on the other hand, the report remains as it was approved by the committee, it is completely useless because - i repeat - the european countries already have such legislation and do not need a framework decision by the european parliament.

they meet certain requirements as regards efficacy and safety, as the commissioner has said. the directive, on the one hand, gives full dignity to medicinal products of plant origin and, on the other, finally puts order into a very confused and controversial field. for example, the scope of the directive is clarified, excluding the use of traditional herbs in other sectors such as food, food supplements and cosmetics. in addition, in the interests of consumer health protection, certain quality and good manufacturing practice characteristics are specified which must be met by medicinal herbs produced in the member states of the european union and those imported from third countries. parliament has sought to recognise that medicinal herbs are, even today, an inexhaustible mine of active ingredients to be used for therapeutic purposes. however, while the therapeutic value of medicinal products of plant origin must be recognized, it must not be forgotten that improper use can give rise to a whole range of serious, sometimes unfortunately fatal, undesirable and toxic side effects. in this connection, commissioner, the us food and drug administration has so far recorded some 2900 cases of toxic effects, including 104 deaths, mainly from the abuse of ephedrine, a drug which releases catecholamines, gives tachyarrhythmias and can lead to cardiac arrest. in addition, the food and drug administration has pointed out the lack of quality control of such herbs placed on the market and coming from countries as far away as china and india: unfortunately, most of these are tainted by the presence of various contaminants. this is why parliament and the commission wanted to ensure that the directive is primarily aimed at protecting the health of consumers, on the one hand by requiring high quality and safety standards and, on the other hand, by imposing the obligation to provide simple and clear information on labels and leaflets for the public about potential toxicity and possible interactions with other medicines and other foods. i would draw the commissioner's attention to the fact that traditional medicinal herbs are those used for a period of at least 30 years, of which at least 10 years in the community and 20 years outside the community, as suggested by parliament. as an expert in the field - i am a pharmacologist - i believe that ten years of use in the member states of the community, plus twenty years of use outside the community, is sufficient to assess potential toxic effects. i am therefore in favour of reducing the 15 years provided for in the commission's initial proposal, while i do not agree with the amendment by mr chris davies, which does not provide for at least a period of 10 years of use in the european union, also because, on the basis of the genetic situation of the various populations, serious toxic effects may emerge without prolonged use in the member states. another positive aspect is the establishment of a committee on medicinal herbs. as you have said, mr commissioner, parliament wants this committee to have the same autonomy and powers as the committee on the evaluation of medicinal products. i hope that parliament's request will be met in such a way that the emea's work can, as usual, proceed with great serenity and efficiency.

mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i too would like to congratulate the rapporteur on her hard and patient work. today the european parliament can debate and tomorrow, i hope, vote on a report which improves the commission's proposal. it is a thorny issue, as has already been said, because the systems in place vary widely from one country to another on this subject. it ranges from extremely secure situations to the absence of any protection. i believe that the three main objectives of equal treatment contained in the proposal are: equal treatment of temporary workers with other workers with regard to security and professional status; compliance with established social standards in user undertakings, by means of equal treatment in terms of pay and working conditions between temporary workers and comparable workers in user undertakings; recognition of the temporary employment sector as a legitimate professional activity by removing unnecessary restrictions, authorisations and prohibitions. the aim of the directive is therefore to guarantee and harmonise a common minimum level of protection for temporary workers without any discrimination. it is a directive which places temporary work within its own segment of the labour market, recognising its weight and importance without however emphasising it to the point of making it almost the only system of recruitment. i also believe, since lisbon has been mentioned, that this directive should regulate temporary work precisely in such a way as to bring it qualitatively into line with the lisbon objectives.

first hypothesis, at least as far as the majority of the group is concerned. another point i think is important to stress concerns the legislative blockade: we believe that article 308 should be amended because, just as unanimity by the council alone cannot meet the need for flexibility in defining the competences of a europe of 25. moreover, as regards the more specifically executive aspects, we are opposed to the idea of a special body or specialized agencies to monitor the technical application of community law: the experience in this respect has been almost always negative. commission. – mr president, today, the commission has adopted a comprehensive analysis of the member states' strategies for ensuring adequate and sustainable pensions. this report is the fruit of a new form of cooperation between the member states, given the consensus that pension systems should remain a responsibility of the member states, and so the role of the european union will be limited to supporting the member states in their reform efforts. this is, of course, without prejudice to the community policies in a number of areas which have an impact on national policy-makers, including internal market policy and the sustainability of public finances, which is examined in the framework of the broad economic policy guidelines. moreover, the financial sustainability of pensions depends very much on the success of the european employment strategy. i am very pleased that the european parliament supports this approach, even though we have yet to find a satisfactory way of involving parliament more in the open method of coordination. the agreement on applying the open method of coordination to the issue of pensions was reached at the laeken european council one year ago. on that occasion, 11 common objectives were set covering the adequacy of pensions, their financial sustainability and the modernisation of pension systems to adapt them to changes on the labour market and in society, notably to ensure that they cater well for the needs of women. an important concept of the whole report is that there are three different dimensions: sustainability, modernisation and adequacy of pensions. it is not just the one dimension that we had until now in our european policies, which was within the framework of public finances. it was also agreed that the member states would submit national strategy reports in which they explain how they achieve those common objectives. the national reports were submitted in september, and the document that has been adopted by the commission today is an analysis of the national strategies, objective by objective. the commission's aim was not to establish a ranking of member states or to lecture them. the open method of coordination on pensions is not a beauty contest. member states have to decide for themselves what type of pension systems they want. but our report tried to highlight certain and concrete strengths and weaknesses of national systems and policies. the common objectives can be achieved through a wide range of pension systems. member states have either flat-rate public pension schemes covering all residents, or earnings-related schemes where benefits are based on employment. they rely to varying degrees on private-funded provision to complement these public schemes. the social partners play a more or less important role in national pension systems. the fact that, in spite of this diversity of systems, we could agree on a set of common objectives proves that it makes sense to speak of a european social model. the diversity of pension systems does not prevent us from having shared goals in this important policy area. in general, the national strategy reports described the current state of play rather than presenting new policy initiatives. the member states involved not just different government departments in their preparation, but also social partners and other interested parties and, in some cases, there has been approval by the national parliaments. one important conclusion that we can draw from this exercise is that member states can cope with ageing societies and avoid a financial or social disaster in their pension systems. the report tries to be neither unduly alarmist, nor too complacent about the situation of pension systems. indeed, there are a lot of positive developments highlighted in the report, but there are also considerable weaknesses. in many countries, the sound financing of future pension benefits has not been secured. one very effective way of achieving this would be to raise the effective retirement age. in fact, achieving the barcelona target of raising the labour market withdrawal age by five years would almost solve our financing problems as identified in the public pension expenditure projections by the economic policy committee. however, we will only get there if member states make much more determined efforts not only to encourage older people to stay longer in the labour market but also to enable them to do so. the european parliament rightly insisted on the importance of health and safety in this regard and on the need to adapt the working environment to the special needs of older workers. many member states also have to do more to improve access to occupational pension schemes, particularly for atypical workers, among whom women tend to be over-represented. the portability of occupational pension rights also requires further improvements, and we will be discussing with the social partners at european level how this could be promoted. the european parliament insisted particularly on the situation of older women. women tend to live longer than men; so a majority of pensioners are women: some 60% of people over 65 and nearly two thirds of people over 75. the gender dimension therefore receives much attention in this report. we can expect individual pension rights for women to increase, thanks to increased labour force participation and smaller pay gaps between men and women. however, career breaks still tend to be taken more often by women than by men. so it will remain important to award pension rights for child-care periods and to maintain derived rights, without which many older women would be exposed to the risk of poverty. however, our priority should be to increase individual pension rights by offering better employment opportunities to women. what is going to happen next with this report? the european council requested a joint report by the commission and the council. so the next step will be to examine the commission's text in the council so as to finalise a report in time for the european council meeting in march. there is no commitment to a second round of national strategy reports and their assessment at european level. however, we are committed to reviewing the common objectives and working methods before 2005 as a basis for deciding on the future of this cooperation. we intend to cooperate with the applicant countries and to carry out the same exercise for their systems. we are also working on common indicators which would allow us to measure the achievements of member states. however, agreement on common indicators is quite a difficult issue and could not be arrived at in time for this report.
mr president, commissioner, i very much appreciate this report from a certain point of view, because it points out that there is a double problem with regard to social security systems: financial sustainability and adequacy. we - and i am thinking of countries like germany or, above all, italy - are preparing generations of poor pensioners. we 'll ask for more and more contributions to make up for ever-lower pensions . we will ask for a titanic additional effort of supplementary contributions. i think this report is overly optimistic. i don't think it's about being alarmists; we must see and point out the reality as it is, and reality says that in europe - i am thinking above all of countries, i repeat, such as italy and germany - we are preparing poor pensioners, we are preparing new budget holes. i fear that you have placed too much trust in the forecasts of the nation states.

madam president, the destruction of cultural heritage is a wound that is constantly open to the palestinians: between 1948 and 1952, the israeli government destroyed 420 palestinian villages, documented by israeli historians. some arab neighborhoods of jaffa were destroyed; in 1967, after the occupation of east jerusalem, the moroccan quarter of the old city was demolished to make way for a large square in front of the western wall. in all these years of military occupation, it has never been allowed to restore the old quarters of the different cities. after the oslo accords and the presence of the palestinian authority, the restoration of the ancient centres of nablus, bethlehem and hebron began with great enthusiasm. in the last two years, with the reoccupation of the autonomous territories, the violence of israeli tanks and bombings has been immense. in nablus, in the historic center, sixty-six buildings built between the 13th and 18th centuries were destroyed, including the caravanserai, the turkish bath, and the ancient soap factories. today, it's the turn of the jaber neighborhood of hebron where the houses are adjacent to the tomb of the patriarchs: mamluk, ottoman, british mandate houses, and so on and so forth. but it is not just about preserving ancient structures: the historic centres are inhabited by women, men and children, like those in the refugee camps of jenin and rafah, which have been left without a roof. and it's over 15,000 in the last two years. the official reason given by the israeli authorities for the military decree that provides for the destruction of the houses in hebron is security and military reasons. nothing more false than that: sharon has made it clear that the qiriat arba colony must be joined to the tomb of the patriarchs. and this is annexation of territory because the settlements in qiriat arba are illegal. it is true that the destruction of the jaber neighbourhood, which is the subject of our resolution today, was decided after an armed action by a palestinian group killed nine people, army soldiers and armed settler guards; it is true that in some cases the destroyed houses in the west bank belong to families whose son, brother or cousin made the tragic and horrible choice to kill himself and israeli civilians, but there are more than two thousand houses destroyed in the last two years! this does not give the right to violate international law and the geneva convention which clearly states the prohibition of collective punishment, the destruction of property, the killing of civilians. over two thousand homes destroyed in the last two years and twenty thousand injured; unfortunately, many israelis have also died, more than 600 now. israel is the occupying country that violates the obligation established by the fourth geneva convention to transfer its population to the occupied territory. there are more than 400 thousand settlers today and it should guarantee the well-being and needs of the palestinian population, while 72 percent are unemployed and locked in the villages. the first illegality is the military occupation of the west bank and gaza, which has been going on since 1967. it cannot be allowed to continue to violate all international law, causing pain and suffering not only to the palestinians but also to its own people. we must send a signal to the palestinians so that they can have hope for justice and prevent the growth of extremism; a signal to the israeli government that it cannot always act outside and beyond the law, raising the threat of anti-semitism and terrorism. we are only willing to have no double standards: human rights and the right to life are equal for all. today's resolution sets a limit: stop the destruction. we stand with those israelis who, together with the palestinians, have lodged an appeal against the demolition of the houses in hebron and who will be demonstrating in this city tomorrow, because the cultural heritage of hebron and palestine is a heritage that belongs to humanity and must be preserved, not destroyed.

the colleagues who preceded me have spoken about it. there was a glimmer of hope in some quarters three months ago when kelsang gyaltsen and lodi gyari, the dalai lama's envoys, returned to beijing for the first official visit in a very long time. meanwhile, a small change has taken place in the people's republic of china. hu jintao has become the new general secretary of the chinese communist party. the so-called dialogue that has been initiated has resulted in the death sentences of tenzin delek and lobsang dhondup. as a sign of dialogue, of course, mrs gebhardt, there is better. that said, i think that we members of the european parliament and we europeans should ask ourselves how we can support the tibetan people. i think we have to ask ourselves this question seriously. there is a risk of exoticism, just as there is a risk that the peaceful struggle of our tibetan friends will not be up to the task of liberating tibet. a goal of the tibetans, but also a goal of all free men and women around the world. our parliament voted almost three years ago, in june 2000, a resolution calling on the governments of the member states to recognise the tibetan government in exile, the dalai lama. i think that this is the way in which we can really give our tibetan friends strength and show our chinese friends that the rule of law is built on a solid foundation of dialogue, and not just on the appearance of dialogue, on those bits of dialogue that they throw at the tibetans and at us europeans, to make us believe, as they have done for the last 40 years, that they want to have dialogue, when every time they refuse real dialogue and any political solution. the president of the tibetan parliament in exile, professor samdhong rimpoche, has asked for restraint until june. i will hold off until june, but i think that from june onwards we will have to reconsider our full support for the battle for the freedom of tibet.
